data.title: MRVL To Post Q3 Earnings: Time To Buy, Sell Or Hold The Stock?
data.description:
Marvell Technology, Inc. (MRVL - Free Report) is scheduled to report third-quarter fiscal 2027 results after market close on Dec. 1, 2026.

For the third quarter of fiscal 2027, Marvell forecasts revenues of $3.15 billion (+/-5%), implying about 15% sequential growth at the midpoint. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for MRVL’s fiscal third-quarter revenues is pegged at $3.16 billion, indicating year-over-year growth of 52.2%.

MRVL projects non-GAAP earnings of $1.10 per share (+/-5 cents). The Zacks Consensus Estimate for MRVL’s fiscal third-quarter earnings is pegged at $1.10 per share, reflecting a 44.7% increase year over year. The consensus mark for earnings has remained unchanged over the past 60 days.

In the trailing four quarters, Marvell’s earnings surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate in three of the trailing four quarters, while matching the same on one occasion, with an average surprise of 0.92%.

Earnings Whispers for MRVL Stock

Our proven model does not conclusively predict an earnings beat for Marvell this time. The combination of a positive Earnings ESP and a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), 2 (Buy) or 3 (Hold) increases the odds of an earnings beat, which is not the case here.

Though Marvell currently carries a Zacks Rank of 3, it has an Earnings ESP of 0.00%. You can uncover the best stocks before they are reported with our Earnings ESP Filter.

Factors Likely to Influence Marvell’s Q3 Results

Marvell’s data center business is likely to have remained the primary growth driver in the third quarter of fiscal 2027, supported by sustained investments in AI infrastructure and rising demand for semiconductor solutions that connect and scale increasingly complex AI systems.

Marvell’s custom silicon business is likely to have remained an important contributor in the to-be-reported quarter. Hyperscalers are increasingly developing specialized AI accelerators and supporting infrastructure to improve computing performance, power efficiency and control over their workloads. This trend is expected to have supported demand for Marvell’s customized XPU and XPU-attach solutions.

Interconnect demand is also likely to have remained strong in the third quarter of fiscal 2027 as AI clusters expand and require greater bandwidth, lower latency and more efficient data movement. Marvell is likely to have benefited from continued adoption of high-speed optical technologies as AI infrastructure evolves beyond conventional scale-out architectures toward scale-up and scale-across configurations.

MRVL’s switching business is also likely to have benefited from increasing networking requirements within AI data centers. As AI workloads become more distributed across larger clusters, efficient Ethernet switching and high-bandwidth networking are becoming increasingly important.

Memory connectivity and expansion are likely to have provided another source of growth in the to-be-reported quarter. Increasing AI inference workloads are creating demand for greater memory capacity and bandwidth, encouraging hyperscalers to explore solutions that improve memory utilization and access.

MRVL Stock Price Performance & Valuation

In the past one year, MRVL shares have gained 52.3%, outperforming the Zacks Electronics – Semiconductors industry’s decline of 15.5%.

MRVL One-Year Performance Chart

Now, let’s look at the value Marvell offers investors at the current levels. MRVL stock trades at a premium price with a forward 12-month price-to-sales (P/S) multiple of 6.33X compared with the industry’s 2.56X.

MRVL Forward 12-Month (P/S) Valuation Chart

MRVL’s Investment Thesis

MRVL’s broad exposure to custom silicon, optical interconnects, switching and memory connectivity is likely to position it to benefit from the expansion of AI computing infrastructure. Management’s improved growth outlook for fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028 also reflects the expanding opportunities across these markets.

The company’s expanding relationships with hyperscalers, alongside a broader pipeline of programs spanning AI accelerators, storage controllers, network interface controllers and memory solutions, should strengthen its growth prospects. Management expects custom silicon demand to accelerate in the second half of fiscal 2027, providing an additional growth catalyst.

Demand for higher-speed optical connectivity, retimers and active electrical cables should therefore remain an important growth driver. The company's recent product launches targeting next-generation AI connectivity further expand its opportunities across these applications. In the meantime, MRVL faces stiff competition from other players as well.

Marvell faces stiff competition in the networking and custom silicon space from Broadcom (AVGO - Free Report) , Astera Labs (ALAB - Free Report) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD - Free Report). Broadcom is a leader in the domain of custom silicon solutions for data centers. Broadcom’s advanced 3.5D XDSiP packaging platform is critical to ensure the performance and efficiency of custom AI XPUs. Advanced Micro Devices is another established player in the custom silicon solutions and AI accelerator market.

Advanced Micro Devices offers semi-custom SoCs and Instinct Accelerators to power data centers. Astera Labs’ Leo CXL smart memory controllers are built for memory expansion up to two terabytes and improve interoperability to accelerate AI performance and cloud computing. The competition from Broadcom, Astera Labs and Advanced Micro Devices has led MRVL to scale up its product delivery faster.

While MRVL is scaling into higher-value AI opportunities, the margin profile can vary with the pace of custom ramp-ups, competitive pricing and the mix of optics, switching and silicon content. Nevertheless, MRVL is prioritizing rapid growth across custom silicon, optical interconnects and switching.

Conclusion: Marvell is well positioned to benefit from sustained AI infrastructure investments, supported by growing opportunities in custom silicon, optical interconnects, switching and memory connectivity. Its expanding hyperscaler relationships and accelerating custom silicon pipeline provide encouraging long-term growth prospects. However, intensifying competition from Broadcom, Advanced Micro Devices and Astera Labs, alongside potential gross margin pressure from changing product mix, remains a concern. Moreover, MRVL’s premium valuation limits its near-term upside potential. With strong growth prospects largely reflected in its valuation, investors may prefer to retain existing positions rather than initiate fresh ones. Hence, we recommend holding MRVL stock.

data.title: The Next AI Giants Could Be Tiny
data.description:
In the 1960s, computers were so big and expensive that only governments, universities and the largest corporations could afford them.

Then came the personal computer. And within a few decades, billions of people had access to computing power that was once reserved for some of the world’s most powerful institutions.

It was one of the most important technological developments of our lifetimes. And it created enormous fortunes for investors who saw it coming.

Today, I believe we’re approaching a similar moment with artificial intelligence.

You see, up until now, the AI boom has largely revolved around a handful of tech giants building massive data centers.

But I’m starting to see evidence that the next wave of AI investment could take us in the opposite direction.

And that could open up an entirely new market for some of America’s smallest technology companies.

The Push for AI Independence

When you ask ChatGPT a question, your request is typically sent over the internet to a data center where powerful computer chips process it and send you back an answer.

I’m not particularly concerned about where my data goes when I ask ChatGPT to help me plan a vacation or recommend a good book.

But consider what happens when a pharmaceutical company wants to use AI to develop a new drug. Or when an aerospace company wants to use it to design a more efficient jet engine.

These companies spend billions of dollars developing products that they don’t want their competitors to know anything about.

And they’re understandably concerned about sending that information outside their own computer networks.

Even the legal protections surrounding that information are being called into question.

Earlier this year, a federal judge ruled that a defendant’s conversations with the AI chatbot Claude weren’t protected by attorney-client privilege.

While companies can use cloud-based AI securely, cases like this help explain why some businesses want more control over their data.

And I’m hearing more about this from some of the biggest names in the AI industry.

In a recent letter to shareholders, Palantir Technologies (Nasdaq: PLTR) CEO Alex Karp wrote: “A global movement is emerging. The revolution for independence and AI sovereignty is now well underway.”

AI sovereignty is essentially the ability to control your own AI systems and the data they use.

For a business, that could mean running AI on its own computers to keep sensitive information within its private network.

And thanks to some recent advances in AI technology, that’s becoming a much more practical option.

You see, there’s a big difference between training an AI model and actually using one.

Training a powerful AI model can require thousands of expensive computer chips working together for months at a time. But once that model has been trained, it can often run on far less powerful equipment.

Using a trained AI model to perform a task is known as inference.

And as you can see in the chart below, spending on AI inference is projected to overtake spending on AI training by 2030.

Source: Bloomberg Intelligence, Morgan Stanley Investment Management, August 2025.
Recreated using approximate chart values.

That’s particularly exciting because inference can often take place outside the massive data centers where AI models are trained.

And researchers are getting better at developing smaller AI models that can perform specific tasks extremely well.

A hospital, for example, doesn’t necessarily need an AI model that can write poetry, translate dozens of languages and explain quantum physics. It might simply need one that can analyze medical images or help doctors review patient records.

Running that AI locally could allow the hospital to process sensitive patient information without sending it to an outside company.

There are other advantages, too.

A manufacturer using AI to inspect products as they move down an assembly line needs to identify defects in real time.

Processing that information locally can reduce delays and allow the system to keep working even if its internet connection goes down.

Then there’s the challenge of building enough data centers to meet the world’s demand for AI.

As I’ve written about before, communities across America are pushing back against data center construction because of concerns about electricity prices, water consumption and the strain these facilities put on local infrastructure.

And even when developers find communities willing to welcome them, getting enough electricity to power these enormous facilities can take years.

So there’s a growing incentive to find ways to bring computing power directly to the businesses that need it.

And the potential market is enormous.

Morgan Stanley estimates that AI could eventually create a $40 trillion market opportunity.

Even a small fraction of that could represent an enormous opportunity for companies supplying businesses with their own AI infrastructure.

Here’s My Take

I still expect the world’s biggest tech companies to spend enormous amounts of money building data centers over the next several years.

But I also believe that we’re going to see a lot more businesses invest in their own AI infrastructure.

And that has exciting implications for investors.

Think back to the personal computer revolution. IBM (IBM) was already a giant in the computer industry when companies like Microsoft (MSFT) and Apple (AAPL) were just getting started.

But the emergence of a whole new market for computers gave these smaller companies an opportunity to become giants in their own right.

I’ve been researching several small technology companies that are developing solutions to help businesses gain greater control over their artificial intelligence.

And on Monday, I’ll show you how a remarkable invention from 20 years ago could help make it possible.

data.title: Firmer Stocks And Oil Leave The Dollar Mixed
data.description:
The US dollar is mixed against the G10 currencies. The Antipodeans and Norwegian krone are leading the advancers, while the yen and Swiss franc are the laggards, perhaps encouraged by the greater appetite for risk as equities are trading firmly today. US index futures rose yesterday during the holiday, but Beijing’s support for Chinese equities also appears to have helped sentiment.  South Korea’s delivered the expected rate hike and signaled more to come yesterday. It did not stand in the way of the Kospi’s 4.35% surge today. 

Rising equities and oil prices—January WTI is trading at its best level since the middle of last week—have weighed on bonds. Rates are firmer in the Asia Pacific region and in Europe.  French bonds are the notable exception.  US 10-year yields are around five basis points higher, and they have not risen on a closing basis for two weeks.  

Prices 

G10

• The euro traded sideways in quiet turnover yesterday. In finished little changed. The week’s high is slightly above $1.1005, but the single currency has not settled above $1.10 since November 9. The downside momentum has faded this week, and the euro is consolidating between about $1.0955 and $1.0985. Around 1.4 bln euro of options struck in the $1.1000-$1.1010 area expire today. 

• The dollar spent this week inside the range established last Friday (~JPY158.40-JPY159.85) against the Japanese yen. The dollar’s resilience is notable given that the US 10-year yield has not risen since November 13. The two-year Treasury yield has fallen 15 bp since then. Moreover, in these past two weeks the swaps market has shaved the odds of a Dec rate hike to a little less than 80% from 85%. 

• For its part, sterling has remained in the range established Monday (~$1.3010-$1.3145). The downside momentum that saw it lose five cents from the high set early November has eased and sterling is trading in the upper end of this week’s range in Europe.  It must reestablish a foothold above $1.3145 to be of note. 

• The Canadian dollar consolidated in a narrow range yesterday after reached a two-week high on Wednesday. The US dollar pulled back from the year’s high on Monday (~CAD1.4385) and overshot the (38.2%) of the rally from the early November low (~CAD1.3930), which is near CAD1.4210. However, it did not settle below it on Wednesday and held it yesterday. The greenback rose slightly above CAD1.4250 yesterday and edged a little higher today before steadying.  Support is seen int eh CAD1.4200-10 area. 

• The Australian dollar spiked to about $0.6560 on Wednesday, a new low for the year, but recovered and settled slightly above $0.6625. News that private capex surged by 12.2% in Q3 (median forecast in Bloomberg’s survey was 4.3%), and Q2’s contraction of -3.6% was revised to -2.0%), helped the Aussie turn in a firm showing yesterday, but it remained below Wednesday’s high (~$0.6665). The daily momentum indicators are turning higher from oversold territory, and the Aussie matched a six-day high today, slightly above $0.6680. A weekly close above $0.6700 would lift the technical tone. Options for about A$625 mln struck at $0.6700 expire today. 

EM 

• The beleaguered Mexican peso fell to a new low for the year on Wednesday as the two-month slide was extended. It consolidated with a soft bias yesterday. The US dollar spiked to almost MXN19.85 on Wednesday. It settled near MXN19.5950 and reached nearly MXN19.7550 yesterday. Encouraged by the upward revision of the central bank’s growth forecast yesterday (1.9% vs 1.5%), and the risk on mood, the dollar has pulled back to around MXN19.4725 today.  A break of MXN19.45 could spur a move toward MXN19.30.  Separately, yesterday Brazil’s President Lula named the Bradesco Chair Trabuco as the new finance minister and the market greeted the news favorably, The Brazilian real strengthened for the fourth consecutive session yesterday. The dollar gapped lower and settled on its low (~BRL5.6610). Initial support may be around BRL5.60.

• The dollar posted its lowest settlement against the offshore yuan yesterday since November 2 (~CNH6.6620). The dollar has been sold to almost CNH6.6535 today. It appeared to have been helped by an unusual statement in the middle of the day indicating official support for the stock market. Despite the new tariffs and controls on offshore data centers that use high-end US-designed chips, Beijing has not retaliated via the exchange rate as some feared. The PBOC set the dollar’s fix at CNY6.7075 today, a new low since July 2022.  (CNY6.7096 yesterday and CNY6.7131 last Friday). 

• Higher oil prices and firmer tech shares weighed on the Indian rupee yesterday after it rose nearly 0.75% on Wednesday, its largest gain in more than a month. The rupee weakened further today, and the dollar tested the INR93.00 in late turnover. 

Other Markets

• Asia Pacific and European equities were mostly higher yesterday. Encouraged by gains in the US index futures and Beijing’s statement, Asia Pacific equities rose today.  China led the wat with a nearly 4.2% rise in the CSI 300. South Korea’s Kospi rose 4.3%. The main exception with Indian indices where slid a little more than 1%. Europe’s Stoxx 600 is rising by more than 1% for the second consecutive session and the third time this week. US Nasdaq 100 and the S&P 500 futures are around 2.6% and 2% better, respectively. 

• Benchmark 10-year yields were a little softer in Japan and the Antipodeans yesterday while they rose mostly 2- 4 in Europe. Italy’s 10-year yield slipped a little less than two basis points yesterday. Yields are rising today.   European rates are mostly 1-3 bp higher.  Softer French inflation is helping support French bonds.  Australian and New Zealand yields rose 2-3 bp earlier.  The 10-year US Treasury yield is up a little more than five basis points to push back above 4.90%. 

• After staging an impressive recovery from slightly below $3427 on Wednesday, gold saw a little follow-through yesterday. It poked above $3607 but could not sustain the momentum and retreated to settle near $3578. However, today, it jumped to $3685 to approach the week’s high, almost $3690.  Silver managed to retain the momentum yesterday that saw it recover from almost $38.20 on Wednesday. It reached nearly $42.30 yesterday and held on to a 1.25% gain. Follow-through buying lifted silver to a new high for the week, almost $44.60. 

• January WTI reached a seven-session high yesterday near $85.25. It bottomed on Tuesday a little above $79, its lowest level since the end of August. It has continued to rise today, and reached $86.60 in Asia Pacific turnover, its best level since November 16. It stalled and pulled back toward $85.20 in Europe. A close above $85 would lift the technical tone. The next target could be around $86.80 and then $88.20. 


Data

• The US reports the advanced goods trade (deficit) for October. Through September, the US has recorded a monthly trade deficit of about $73.6 bln. With the tariff frontloading last year, the average monthly shortfall was nearly $83.9 bln in the first nine months of 2025 and $70.3 bln in Jan-Sept 2024. The goods deficit was $135.1 bln in September. Also, October retail and wholesale inventories will be reported. Trade and inventories are among the more volatile components of GDP and with today’s reports, economists may adjust Q4 GDP projections. The median forecast in Bloomberg’s survey is for 2.2% growth (3.4% in Q3). 

• Canada reports its Q3 current account. The median forecast in Bloomberg’s survey is for a C$9.4 bln surplus after an $8.8 bln surplus in Q2. The quarterly average in H1 26 was C$0.26 bln, which is the first two-quarter surplus since H1 22. 

• Mexico reports its October trade balance today. The median forecast in Bloomberg’s survey is for a $2.1 bln surplus. In the first nine months of the year, Mexico has reported an average monthly surplus of $1.03 bln compared with an average deficit of $377.6 mln in the Jan-Sept 2025 period and a $2.2 bln deficit in the same period in 2024. 

• The ECB’s inflation survey found higher expectations in last month’s survey. The one-year expectation is 3.5% (3.1% previously), and the three-year expectations edged up to 3.0% from 2.9%. Still, the preliminary French and Spanish November CPI readings were lower than expected. France’s harmonized November CPI fell 0.7% (-0.4% expected) and the year-over-year rate fell to 3.2% from 3.7%. Spain’s harmonized measures also fell by 0.7%. The year-over-year pace slackened to 4.1% from 4.9%. Note that Spain goes to the polls this weekend and the People’s Party looks set to replace the Socialist Sanchez government. The rub is that it may need the support of the far-right VOX to secure a majority. Separately, the EU November confidence surveys were mostly softer. 

• Tokyo’s November CPI rose a bit less than expected. The headline pace ticked up to 2.8% from 2.7%. It has not fallen since May. The core measure rose to 2.9% from 2.6%, while the measure that excludes fresh food and energy slipped to 2.5% from 2.6%. The national figures are not released until December 18, the same day the BOJ meeting concludes. The swaps market has almost 80% of a quarter-point hike discounted. 

• China reported October industrial profits earlier today. Year-to-date, year-over-year, industrial profits rose 16.0% from 15.5% in September. The year-over-year rate stands at 20.1% (14.4% in September).

data.title: Asia Week Ahead: RBI Rate Hike, And Data On China, Japan, Korea
data.description:
Markets will watch the Reserve Bank of India’s expected 25bp rate hike, while keeping a close eye on China’s PMIs, activity indicators from Japan and South Korea, Philippine inflation data, and Taiwan’s local elections.

India: RBI to hike rates 25bp amid persistent inflation

We expect the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to raise its policy rate by 25bp on Friday, as both headline and core inflation have moved above the central bank’s target, strengthening the case for further tightening. While lower fuel prices should ease headline inflation in the months ahead, food remains a key concern in India. It poses upside risks to inflation expectations and keeps underlying price pressures elevated. As a result, core inflation is likely to remain relatively sticky.

Philippines: Headline inflation to ease as fuel prices fall

Philippine CPI inflation should ease further, reflecting sharp declines in fuel prices. Gasoline and diesel have recorded consecutive weekly cuts, with average gasoline prices down around 11% in November versus October, providing meaningful drag on headline inflation. Core inflation, however, is likely to remain relatively sticky, supported by still-firm services costs and underlying domestic demand.

China: Manufacturing to improve but remain in contraction

China published November purchasing managers’ index data. We’re looking for the manufacturing PMI to rebound to 49.5 in November, up from 49.3, but remain in contraction territory. Industrial production cooled slightly in October. Ideally, we’d see better momentum in November. The non-manufacturing PMI is expected to fare slightly better, coming in at 49.7, stable from October.

Taiwan: Local elections in focus

No significant data releases are expected for Taiwan in the week ahead. However, local elections over the weekend will be the key event to watch. Though these elections may often be driven more by local issues than national politics, they will still serve as a check on relative support for the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and Kuomintang (KMT).

Korea: Trade strength and inflation in focus

South Korea will release October industrial production data on Monday. The market expects annual growth to accelerate to 14.5% year-on-year, from 1.2% in September. Month-on-month, output is forecast to decline 0.6% after the previous month’s 9.0% increase.

November trade data are due on Tuesday. Exports and imports are expected to grow 98.9% and 38.8% YoY, respectively, supported by robust semiconductor and AI-related demand. The trade surplus is forecast to widen to $48.6bn, from a revised $42.7bn in October.

Korea releases November CPI data on Wednesday. The market expects headline inflation to ease to 2.7% YoY, from 2.8% in October. Persistent above-target inflation would support the Bank of Korea’s continued tightening bias following its November rate hike.

Japan: Retail sales, IP and capital spending in focus

Japan releases October retail sales and industrial production data on Monday. The market expects retail sales growth to rise to 2.7% YoY, from a revised 2.4% in September. The improvement would suggest that household consumption is recovering gradually, although elevated living costs and higher borrowing costs remain headwinds. Industrial production is expected to rise 2.1% MoM in October, broadly in line with September’s 2.0% increase. Year-on-year, the market expects industrial production growth to accelerate to 2.7% from 1.7%, indicating that manufacturing activity remains resilient.

Japan will also release third-quarter capital spending data on Monday. The market expects capital spending growth to accelerate to 4.3% YoY, from 1.6% in the second quarter. The expected pickup would suggest that corporate investment remains resilient despite higher borrowing costs.

data.title: Dell Delivers Record Results, But Wall Street Sees A Catch
data.description:
Dell Technologies delivered another record quarter, raised its annual forecasts and authorized billions in additional share buybacks. Yet Wall Street initially reacted by selling the stock.

Reuters reported Wednesday, Nov. 25, that Dell Technologies (DELL) shares fell 5.7% in early trading despite the company’s stronger outlook and an additional $25 billion share repurchase authorization. The stock later recovered, closing 0.6% higher at $297.06.

The erratic response followed the exceptional profits report.

Driven by the increasing demand for AI servers, Dell’s fiscal third-quarter sales more than doubled to a record $54.9 billion.

Additionally, the corporation revised its full-year sales prediction higher for the third time this year, from $192 billion to $202 billion.

Reuters reported Tuesday that the new forecast exceeded analysts’ expectations of approximately $194.5 billion.

However, the market’s initial reaction reflected growing apprehension about the massive expenditures required to sustain AI growth.

Investors are becoming more skeptical of technology firms’ ability to turn their infrastructure investments into long-term earnings.

For Dell shareholders, the tension is striking: The company is reporting record demand, but investors still want convincing evidence that the growth can last.

Dell’s AI server business delivers record results

Dell’s most recent financial results show how drastically AI has changed the company’s operations.

For the fiscal third quarter, the firm posted adjusted profits of $9.45 per share, which was higher than analysts’ projections of $6.59 and up 265% from the same period last year.

Dell’s Infrastructure Solutions Group generated $42 billion in revenue, representing a 198% annual increase, according to its Nov. 24 earnings release.

The company’s major financial highlights included:

  • Total revenue: $54.9 billion, up 103%.

  • AI server revenue: $22 billion, up 291%.

  • Traditional server and networking revenue: $15 billion, up 235%.

  • Storage revenue: $4.9 billion, up 24%.

  • Adjusted earnings per share: $9.45, up 265%.

  • AI server backlog: $132.3 billion.

Dell received $60.2 billion in AI server orders in the quarter, indicating continued computing infrastructure growth.

Jeff Clarke, COO, said the company evaluates orders based on customer quality, financing capacity, and infrastructure.

The large backlog gives Dell visibility into future demand, but orders must be fulfilled and revenue generated.

Why Wall Street remains cautious about Dell

Dell’s earnings come amid growing skepticism about the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending.

Reuters reported Wednesday that technology stocks faced renewed pressure as investors questioned the financing behind large data center expansions.

These worries have impacted businesses that provide servers, processors, and other equipment.

In addition, growing memory prices and concerns about future profitability put pressure on Dell.

The company’s infrastructure operating margin reached 17%, up from 12.4% a year earlier, although investors remain concerned about the outlook for hardware margins.

Another issue is Dell’s conventional PC business.

Although operating income fell by 6%, its Client Solutions Group’s sales increased by 3% to $12.9 billion.

Dell’s quarterly figures show that consumer PC sales dropped 15% to around $1.6 billion.

The disparity shows how much business infrastructure investment, as opposed to regular PC customers, now drives Dell’s growth.

Dell’s $25 billion buyback sends a different message

Dell’s management is expressing confidence in the company’s financial prospects, despite the market’s initial pessimism.

The board expanded its current buyback program by approving an extra $25 billion in share repurchases.

Dell also returned a record $4.9 billion to shareholders through dividends and repurchases during the quarter.

Dell has not yet acquired $25 billion worth of shares as a result of the expanded authorization. Over time, it increases management’s ability to buy back shares.

Although the financial advantages depend on purchase price and execution, buybacks may reduce the number of outstanding shares and perhaps increase per-share profits.

Although the permission is a positive signal for investors, the dangers associated with future AI expenditure remain.

What Dell’s latest forecast means for shareholders

Dell now expects fiscal 2027 AI server revenue of $78 billion, up from its previous $74 billion forecast.

The company also raised its adjusted annual earnings outlook to $29.68 per share from $25.50.

Fourth-quarter revenue is projected to reach approximately $56.3 billion, with adjusted earnings of $8.40 per share.

These numbers imply that management anticipates a continued high demand for AI infrastructure.

The next challenge, meanwhile, is whether Dell can maintain its profitability while fulfilling a record backlog and controlling growing component prices.

Wednesday’s trade reflected that uncertainty.

Despite its remarkable performance, Dell first sold off, but by the closing bell, it had recovered.

The question of whether Dell can profit from the AI boom is no longer the most important for investors. The question now is whether the business can continue to develop profitably enough to meet Wall Street’s demands.

Gold prices remain under pressure for now, and it likely won’t settle until the current bout of market-wide selling eases.

data.title: Ethereum Glamsterdam Upgrade Cleared For December 15 Test: Will ETH Rally Like After Pectra?
data.description:
On Thursday, November 26, Ethereum’s core developers agreed to take the Ethereum Glamsterdam upgrade to its final public test on December 15, keeping a disputed gas rule exactly as written. The test runs on Hoodi, the network developers use as a dress rehearsal for mainnet.

It comes seven weeks later than planned. An October test was called off after a security firm warned that the new charges could change how programs already running on Ethereum behave. Developers now point to a mainnet launch in late January or early February, though no date is fixed yet.

ETH barely moved on the news. It trades at $1,730, down 42% since January 1. The Fear & Greed index sits at 12, deep in extreme fear, and traders have heard plenty of upgrade stories before.

So does a hard fork still move the ETH price?

Why Was the Ethereum Glamsterdam Test Delayed Until December 15?
The Gas Rule That Delayed the Test

The call summary on Ethereum Magicians records a “rough consensus” among execution teams to ship the current spec unchanged. The fight was over EIP-8037, a rule that adds a separate charge on anything that creates new permanent data on Ethereum, such as a new account or storage slot.

The goal is to stop the “state,” the database every node has to keep, from growing without limit. The price is steep. Creating a new contract today has a flat base cost of 32,000 gas. Under EIP-8037, the storage charge alone would be 183,600 gas, before regular fees.

That change is what worried auditors. ChainSecurity replayed a year of real Ethereum activity and found about 200 problems across bridges, wallets, exchanges, staking services and oracles. Most can be fixed with a setting, but 24 need code upgrades. Ethereum Foundation developer Marius van der Wijden estimates that up to 15,000 of Ethereum’s roughly 90 million contracts could be exposed.

A last-minute plan to simplify how the charges are tracked was turned down. Teams have until December 15 to report serious problems and until January 10 for the rest. Client releases for node operators are due early next week.

What Other Changes Will the Ethereum Glamsterdam Upgrade Bring?

The gas rule grabbed the headlines, but the Ethereum Glamsterdam list in EIP-7773 is long. Two changes matter most for how the network runs.

The first is enshrined proposer-builder separation, or ePBS (EIP-7732). Today, validators who propose blocks mostly buy them from specialist builders. Outside relays sit in the middle of that deal. ePBS moves it into Ethereum’s own rules, cutting out the middlemen that most blocks now depend on.

The second is block-level access lists (EIP-7928). A block will list up front which accounts and storage it touches, so nodes can load data and check transactions in parallel instead of one by one. That is groundwork for raising Ethereum’s capacity later.

Smaller items will please wallets and exchanges. Plain ETH transfers will emit a log, making them easier to track, and the maximum contract size goes up. The Sepolia testnet already switched to Glamsterdam on October 6.

ETH Price After the Last Five Ethereum Upgrades

An upgrade like Ethereum Glamsterdam sounds like good news for the price. The record is more mixed. We measured ETH’s move from the open on each mainnet upgrade day to the close 30 days later and compared it with bitcoin over the same window.

ETH beat bitcoin in the month after three of the five upgrades. The best run came after Pectra in May 2025, when ETH jumped 36% in 30 days while bitcoin added 8%. Shapella, which unlocked staked ETH in April 2023, and Fusaka last December also came out ahead.

The two misses were the most hyped launches. ETH fell 22% in the month after the Merge in September 2022, while bitcoin lost 6%. Dencun followed a 59% run-up in the month before it went live, and ETH then gave back 19%.

Five upgrades is a small sample, and each one met a different market. Still, the record argues against selling the news by reflex. Pectra is the closest match to today: ETH went into it near $1,800 after a long slide, and the price now sits just below that.

ETH Price Analysis: $1,540 Is the Floor to Watch

ETH trades at $1,730, below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $2,066. The 200-day EMA sits higher, at $2,226.

  • Resistance: $1,850, a level ETH traded around in February and August and lost again in mid-November. Above that sits $2,000, the round number that held as a floor in April and turned ETH back in July.

  • Support: $1,540, the zone that held in late June and again on November 21, when ETH dipped to $1,538. Below that sits the 2026 low of $1,505 from June 6.

ETHUSDT 1D chart. Source: TradingView

The Ethereum Glamsterdam test on December 15 is the next real date for ETH. If Hoodi runs cleanly, developers can set a mainnet date in January, and the Pectra comparison will get its first real check.

data.title: Micron Stock Is Highly Undervalued As The Wyckoff Theory Takes Shape
data.description:
Micron stock has slipped into a bear market this month and now appears to be in the Wyckoff theory's markdown phase, even as its key valuation metric has fallen to bargain levels. MU was trading at $601, about 52% below its year-high. So, is this a good time to buy the dip, or should investors sell the rip?

Micron stock has become highly undervalued

In theory, companies that are seeing substantial revenue and profit growth should receive premium valuations. Some of the most popular companies that have always had a premium valuation are Walmart, Costco, and Shopify. 

Micron, however, is doing the opposite. Its revenue growth is soaring, and analysts expect the momentum will continue. The most recent results showed that its fourth-quarter revenue jumped by 379% to $54.2 billion, with its annual figure hitting $133.2 billion. Most of this growth was in its DRAM division, which made $39.8 billion. 

Micron is also a highly profitable company, with the gross margin of all its businesses being over 80%. Its total gross profit margin rose to 87%, much higher than most companies, including Nvidia. 

Most importantly, analysts believe that the company has more room for growth. For example, the first-quarter revenue is expected to hit $61 billion, while the second-quarter figure will soar to $66 billion. Its annual revenue is expected to jump by 106% to $275 billion. 

For a company experiencing this growth, its valuation metrics are significantly low. For example, the forward price-to-earnings ratio stands at just 3.43, much lower than the sector median of 18. 

Similarly, the company has one of the highest rule-of-40 metrics. This multiple is calculated by adding its revenue growth and its profit margins. Micron has a forward revenue growth of 106% and a profit margin of 64%, giving it a multiple of 170%. 

These metrics explain why the company is planning to accelerate its share repurchases in the near term. Its plan is to start a $35 billion program in December when the buyback restrictions end. Share buybacks help to boost a company’s earnings per share by reducing its outstanding shares.

Micron is facing risks

Therefore, the falling Micron stock price and cheaper valuation is happening because of the rising risks in the industry. One of the main risks is that the AI bubble may burst soon. The AI Stock Bubble Index has remained above 60.

There are also concerns that some AI data center companies will find it hard to survive as financing in the industry dries out. Elon Musk has warned that over 200 neocloud companies will collapse.

These fears have risen after the recent Anthropic IPO, in which the company raised over $100 billion. Its stock has plunged afterwards. OpenAI has also struggled in its fundraising. It recently raised $11 billion, much lower the $30 billion it was aiming for. 

There is also a risk that the memory supercycle will end in the coming months or years. Historically, this business is usually made up of major boom-and-bust cycles.

Micron share price is in the markdown phase

The weekly chart shows that MU stock has formed the classic Wyckoff Method. It remained in a consolidation phase for years, a sign that it was in the accumulation phase. 

The stock then entered the markup phase mid-last year and then started its upward trend, eventually reaching a record high of $1,255. Now, there are signs that it has dropped into the markdown phase, which is characterized by panic selling.

Therefore, the stock will likely continue falling in the near term. The next key level to watch will be at the 50-week moving average of $523.

data.title: The Goods Balance Of Trade Is Negative 149.5 Billion, Approaching Largest Ever
data.description:
The Econoday consensus expected an improvement. The result was $14 billion worse.

The Census Bureau Advance Indicators for October show the deficit increased by $14.4 billion.

Advance Goods Data

  • The international trade deficit was $149.5 billion in October, up $14.4 billion from $135.1 billion in September.

  • Exports of goods for October were $215.8 billion, $6.7 billion more than September exports.

  • Imports of goods for October were $365.3 billion, $21.1 billion more than September imports.

I see no reason to compare advance trade data to previous advance numbers now known to be wrong.

So, my chart shows goods from the latest full release (September) plus the advance trade data for October.

Goods Exports and Imports October 2026

October Advance vs September Actuals

  • Exports: 210,968 to 215,819 Up $4.85 billion

  • Imports: 346,879 to 365,297 Up $18.42 billion

  • Net: $4.85 exports minus 18.42 imports = -13.57 billion

If the advance trade numbers are accurate, the next full release will show the goods deficit increasing by ~13.57 billion.

This is a better way of estimating things vs comparing advance numbers to previous advance numbers now revised away with final results.

Biggest Trade Deficit In History

Excluding the enormous trade distortions caused by Trump’s tariffs, we have the largest trade deficit in history.

First, there was a surge of front-running imports and a peak deficit of 159 billion (yellow highlight). Then we had an artificial improvement (green highlight) accompanied by inventory drawdowns.

Now things are back to where they would be without the distortions.

Q: Where is that?
A: Record deficits despite the now obviously ridiculous idea that tariffs would change anything.

Trump also drove Canada closer to China, losing the best trade partner in the process. Meanwhile, businesses suffer from higher prices and the trade deficit is still going up.

Meanwhile, please note that Trump is doubling down with Section 301 tariffs.

No exact effective date has been set yet, and nothing will take effect before late January 2027.

Question of the Day

Q: How distorted is the advance trade data today?
A: Excellent question. We may already be seeing more tariff front running in advance of the new Section 301 tariffs. Discussion below.

Section 301 Procedural Timeline

  • Public comment deadline. Written comments on the proposed rates and product exemptions are due January 5, 2027.

  • U.S.-China trade truce expiration. The current bilateral trade truce (the Busan Agreement) is set to expire on January 10, 2027, which directly affects whether China faces the proposed 20% baseline rate or the 40% fallback rate.

  • Public hearings. USTR will hold public hearings starting January 25, 2027.

  • Final determination and implementation. Any final tariff rates, product carve-outs, and effective dates will be issued only after USTR reviews the January comments and hearing testimony.

Section 301 Key Context

  • Targeted economies. The 14 covered economies are Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, and Vietnam. (Determinations for Mexico and Norway remain pending.)

  • How they interact with July 2026 duties. For economies other than China, the proposed rates are designed to apply net of the 10% to 12.5% Section 301 forced-labor tariffs imposed in July 2026—meaning importers would generally pay the higher of the two rates rather than stacking both.

  • For China, the new rates would stack on top of the 2018 Section 301 tariffs.

So we may be in store for another huge wave of tariff front-running, perhaps already underway.

For discussion of the new Section 301 tariffs, please see Trump Doubles Down on Tariff Stupidity, Leans Nothing from Election

My base case was Trump would act foolishly after the election, already proven.

For import discussion related to AI spending, please see How Much Did AI Spending Contribute to Third-Quarter 2026 GDP?

The charts below show the AI impact for every quarter starting 2025 Q1.

It’s possible, in theory, for the surge in the trade deficit to related to investment gold which the BEA would subtract out as irrelevant. We do not have gold imports and exports breakouts in the advance report.

However, there is little evidence this is gold related. The main import driver was capital goods imports, which rose ~8.5% to about $171.4 billion. That increase accounted for roughly two-thirds of the total import rise and is widely linked to AI infrastructure spending. Capital goods imports are also up ~80% year-over-year.

We do not know how much of that surge was tariff front running.

data.title: Silver Takes The Lead After The Miners' Reversal
data.description:
Yesterday, I wrote that the miners' reversal and volume were "very bullish for the following week." The rally didn't wait.

At the moment of writing these words, December gold futures are at about $3,639, after moving up to $3,683.50 this morning, and December silver futures are at about $43.52, after a high of $44.30. On Wednesday, the day before Thanksgiving, they moved down to $3,425.20 and $37.955, respectively, and then they reversed.

Silver is now leading the rebound, but the mining stocks moved first.

The Miners Moved First

Yesterday's analysis was about Wednesday's reversal in the miners. The GDXJ, which holds junior mining stocks, moved below Friday's low and then closed 10.4 percent above its intraday low, its biggest intraday rebound since April 2020, on big volume. I wrote: "In my view, the size of the reversal and the size of the volume are very bullish for the following week."

This morning, the GDXJ opened at about $92, up from Wednesday's close of $87.66, while the GLD, which tracks gold, opened at about $333, up from $327.45.

One of my Gold Trading Alerts subscribers asked in the comments this morning whether it's time to take profits on the miners, since they're close to my profit-take level while gold and silver are still below their targets. It's a good question, and I'm happy to answer it here as well. In my view, the miners are likely to keep leading, and in today's Gold Trading Alert, I described how I'm adjusting the position for it.

The reason why the miners tend to turn first is worth a closer look.

Why the Miners Lead at Bottoms

Mining stocks are leveraged to the price of gold. A miner's costs don't drop when gold falls, so its profits fall faster than the gold price does, and they rise faster when gold rebounds. Take a miner that produces gold at a cost of $2,000 per ounce. At $3,500 gold, its margin is $1,500 per ounce. At $3,800 gold, it's $1,800, which is 20 percent more, while gold is less than 9 percent higher.

The miners are also stocks, and stocks are priced on what investors expect. When investors think that the worst is priced in, they buy the miners before gold turns.

November 2008 shows the same thing on a bigger scale. Between September 22 and October 24, 2008, the USD Index rallied about 13 percent, while the S&P 500 fell about 27 percent and the GDX about 53 percent. In November, the USD Index moved to new highs, and the S&P 500 fell below its October low, closing at 752.44 on November 20. But on that day, the GDX closed at $18.20, above its October 24 close of $17.80. The next day, it soared 26.5 percent. By the end of 2008, the GDX was at $33.88, about 90 percent above its October 24 close, while gold was about 20 percent higher.

At real bottoms, the miners lead gold higher, but it's a tendency, not a law. This week, the miners led what I view as a corrective upswing, and gold and silver followed.

Gold Reversed Right After Reaching My $3,500 Target

Gold's part of the story started a month ago. On October 30, I wrote: "With the first target reached, the next one is about $3,500." When I wrote it, December gold futures traded near $3,906. On Wednesday, they moved down to $3,425.20, about 12 percent lower, and reversed on the same day.

This morning, December gold futures moved up to $3,683.50, about $258 above Wednesday's low. Zooming in allows us to see clearly that gold broke above its declining, very short-term resistance line.

The dollar didn't help. The USD Index is at about 103.92, up from Wednesday's close of 103.67, and the 10-year Treasury yield rose to about 4.90 percent. Gold rallying while the dollar moves higher and interest rates rise is a bullish sign for the short term.

Silver is rallying even more than gold.

Silver Takes the Lead

Silver's long slide started at a price that I had named in advance. On January 27, I wrote that "we might see another attempt that takes silver to $120 or even a bit above it before a bigger decline". Silver topped almost exactly at $120, and on Wednesday, December silver futures moved down to $37.955, their lowest level since June 2025, about 68 percent below that top.

This morning, they moved up to $44.30, and they're now at about $43.52. Silver moves more than gold in both directions, and when it rallies faster than gold, the gold-to-silver ratio falls. On Wednesday, the ratio moved up to about 90 at the lows. This morning, it's at about 83.

Another subscriber asked in the comments on Wednesday whether the ratio, which was forming a topping candle that day, was worth keeping an eye on. Yes, it is. In declines, silver tends to fall faster than gold, and the ratio rises. In rallies, silver tends to outpace gold, and the ratio falls. So the ratio's reversal from about 90 fits the upswing in the precious metals sector.

There's one more thing that I'm watching. Silver's strength against gold often shows up right before short-term tops. Today, gold and the miners are rising along with silver, so that's not the same signal. If silver soars while gold and the miners lag, I'll view it as a sign that the upswing is maturing.

Where This Leaves Us

The miners reversed first, on Wednesday, and today, silver is leading gold higher, while the gold-to-silver ratio falls from about 90 to about 83. Gold is rallying even though the dollar and Treasury yields are moving higher. In my view, this is a corrective upswing within the medium-term decline, and it's likely to continue for now. In today's Gold Trading Alert, I described how I'm adjusting the position in the miners and what I plan to do after this upswing.

The miners moved first. Now silver is catching up.

Higher Revenue and Adj. FCF Forecasts

It also maintains an allocation to "equity dislocation" which goes long value and short expensive growth names. It also seems like a variation on relative value but either way, equity dislocation reminds me a little of BTAL which is long low beta stocks and short high beta. The GMO Alternative Allocation Fund (GAAGX) is as close to stand alone as I think we can get. Here's the allocation which is obviously levered up.

At first glance, it looks more like an absolute return fund but with a pretty low growth rate.

Maybe, this is like our post the other day where we took the strategy underlying the Cambria Trinity ETF (TRTY) and rebuilt it with different funds.

data.title: AI Shopping Assistants Help You Find Deals. Retailers Like The Bigger Orders.
data.description:
AI shopping assistants promise to save consumers time, find better prices and simplify holiday shopping. For retailers, the technology offers something potentially more valuable: an opportunity to increase customer spending.

Walmart (WMT), Amazon (AMZN) and other major retailers are investing in artificial intelligence to change how consumers discover products, compare prices and make purchasing decisions.

The technology sounds convenient. Tell an AI assistant what you need, provide a budget and receive personalized recommendations within seconds.

But there is a fundamental difference between helping someone find a better deal and helping a retailer sell more merchandise.

Wall Street understands the difference.

AI Shopping Assistants Are Changing Consumer Behavior

Traditional online shopping requires consumers to search for products, compare specifications, read reviews and evaluate prices.

Artificial intelligence reduces much of this work.

Walmart's Sparky shopping assistant helps customers discover products, compare options and receive recommendations. Amazon has also incorporated artificial intelligence into its shopping experience through conversational assistants and product discovery tools.

These systems can recommend complementary products, suggest alternatives and help consumers assemble entire shopping lists.

Consider a customer purchasing a coffee machine for $150.

An AI shopping assistant could recommend coffee filters, specialty coffee, cleaning supplies and an extended warranty.

The customer originally intended to spend $150. After accepting several recommendations, the purchase reaches $220.

The consumer receives a more complete shopping experience. The retailer receives nearly 47% more revenue from the transaction.

Everyone appears satisfied, except perhaps the customer's original budget.

Retailers Have a Financial Incentive to Increase Spending

Retailers closely monitor average order value, conversion rates, customer retention and purchase frequency.

These metrics influence revenue growth, operating profitability and corporate valuations.

AI shopping assistants could improve several of these measures simultaneously.

Personalized recommendations can increase the number of products customers purchase. Faster product discovery can reduce abandoned shopping carts. Automated shopping lists can encourage repeat purchases.

The financial implications become significant when applied across millions of transactions.

Consider a hypothetical retailer processing 100 million annual online orders with an average transaction value of $80.

A 5% increase in average order value would generate an additional $400 million in annual revenue, assuming transaction volume remains unchanged.

Even after accounting for technology expenses, fulfillment costs and promotional discounts, the potential financial benefits explain why retailers are investing heavily in artificial intelligence.

The opportunity extends beyond selling more products. Retailers can use customer interactions to improve inventory management, identify emerging demand and refine marketing strategies.

Amazon and Walmart Are Competing for the Customer's Next Decision

Amazon and Walmart already possess extensive consumer purchasing data.

Artificial intelligence gives both companies additional ways to interpret customer preferences and influence purchasing decisions.

Instead of waiting for shoppers to search for individual products, retailers can present recommendations based on previous purchases, stated preferences and immediate shopping needs.

The competition increasingly involves controlling the interface through which consumers make decisions.

A customer who relies on one shopping assistant for groceries, electronics, household products and holiday gifts has fewer reasons to visit competing websites.

For retailers, this could strengthen customer retention and reduce dependence on traditional digital advertising.

For smaller businesses, the challenge is different.

If consumers increasingly rely on AI-generated recommendations, independent retailers must compete for visibility within those recommendations.

A company can offer a competitive product at an attractive price and still struggle to reach consumers if the shopping assistant prioritizes other options.

Artificial Intelligence Could Reshape Retail Advertising

Retail advertising has become an important business for major e-commerce companies.

Amazon and Walmart operate advertising businesses allowing brands to pay for visibility across their retail platforms.

Conversational shopping assistants introduce another potential advertising opportunity.

Instead of displaying sponsored products alongside traditional search results, retailers could incorporate commercial recommendations into conversational shopping experiences.

This raises important questions about transparency.

When an AI assistant recommends a product, consumers should understand whether the recommendation reflects price, quality, personal preferences or a commercial relationship.

The Federal Trade Commission has established guidance requiring appropriate disclosure of material commercial relationships and advertising practices.

As AI shopping becomes more widespread, regulators could examine how retailers disclose sponsored recommendations and whether consumers understand the commercial incentives behind them.

The distinction between independent advice and advertising becomes increasingly important when both appear inside the same conversation.

Does AI Shopping Save Consumers Money?

Artificial intelligence can help consumers identify discounts, compare product features and reduce the time required to research purchases.

Those benefits are legitimate.

The problem arises when consumers confuse saving money on individual products with reducing their total spending.

A shopper who receives a 20% discount on several unnecessary purchases has still spent money on products they did not originally intend to buy.

Consumers using AI shopping assistants should establish spending limits before requesting recommendations.

They should also compare prices across competing retailers, review subscription offers carefully and distinguish essential purchases from suggested additions.

Convenience should not replace financial discipline.

What Wall Street Should Watch

Investors evaluating AI investments across the retail industry should focus on measurable financial results.

The most important indicators include:

Average order value.

Online conversion rates.

Customer retention.

Digital advertising revenue.

Gross profit margins.

Technology infrastructure expenses.

Operating income growth.

Return on AI-related capital investments.

Higher revenue alone does not establish profitability.

Retailers could increase sales while experiencing higher fulfillment expenses, greater promotional costs and substantial artificial intelligence infrastructure spending.

Investors need evidence of sustainable earnings improvements rather than impressive technology demonstrations.

The companies most likely to benefit are those capable of converting artificial intelligence investments into profitable transactions without damaging consumer trust.

The Bigger Economic Question

Consumer spending accounts for roughly two-thirds of U.S. economic activity.

If AI shopping assistants meaningfully influence purchasing behavior across millions of households, their impact could extend beyond individual retailers.

Higher transaction values could support retail revenue and economic activity. Excessive spending could also increase household financial pressure, particularly among consumers carrying credit card balances.

The long-term economic effect will depend on whether artificial intelligence improves purchasing efficiency or encourages additional consumption.

For now, retailers have a clear incentive to make shopping easier.

Consumers should remember why.

Your AI shopping assistant might find you a better deal. The retailer would still prefer you purchase something else before checking out.

data.title: Jobless Growth: What A Shrinking Workforce Means For Investors
data.description:
Jobless growth is usually a symptom of a weak economy, but this time the economy is growing due to productivity gains even as the workforce shrinks, which changes what investors should watch.

Key Takeaways

  • Real GDP grew by 2.2% in the year to mid-2026 while payroll employment grew just 0.3%. That is jobless growth by any definition.

  • Past episodes of jobless growth came after recessions, with unemployment between 5.6% and 9.1%. Today it’s happening mid-expansion with unemployment at 4.2%.

  • The workforce is shrinking. Participation among Americans 55 and older fell from 38.0% to 36.9% over the past year as boomers retire.

  • With fewer workers, growth has to come from productivity, which rose 2.2% over the past year, slightly above its long-run average of 2.0%.

  • For investors, weak payroll numbers alone are a poor recession signal now. Unemployment, layoffs, and the wealth effect matter more.

Here’s a combination that doesn’t usually last. Over the year to the second quarter of 2026, the U.S. economy grew 2.2% after inflation.1 Over roughly the same stretch, payroll employment grew 0.3%.2 Hiring averaged about 41,000 jobs a month over the 12 months through September, and four of those months were outright negative. Economists call this “jobless growth,” and it has a reputation as a warning sign.

The reputation is earned. Historically, jobless growth showed up after recessions, when companies squeezed more output from fewer workers and refused to hire until they had to. Add American Express announcing 3,500 job cuts on October 23 and the “recession is coming” crowd has plenty of material.3 However, when you look at who is actually leaving the labor force, this version of jobless growth tells a very different story, and it matters for how you read the next jobs report.

What Is Jobless Growth?

Jobless growth is exactly what it sounds like: the economy expands, measured by GDP, while employment barely moves. Normally, the two travel together because more output requires more workers. The chart below shows that relationship over six decades.

Notice in the chart above that the gold line usually tracks the black one. The gaps open in specific places: the early 1990s, the early 2000s, and the years after 2009. Each of those was a “jobless recovery.” Businesses had just lived through a recession, and demand was soft. Companies met rising orders by working existing staff harder rather than adding headcount.

Today’s gap looks similar on the surface. The difference is the unemployment rate sitting underneath it.

Source: BLS and BEA via FRED (GDPC1, PAYEMS, UNRATE). Two-year changes from Q2 (GDP) and June (payrolls). Calculations: RIA Advisors.

The last two rows are almost identical in growth and hiring. In 2011, jobless growth meant millions of people wanted work and couldn’t find it. In 2026, it means there are fewer people looking. Such is the distinction most of the “jobless growth” coverage misses, and it changes the investment conclusion entirely.

Hiring Stalled, But Unemployment Didn’t Rise

If weak hiring reflected weak demand for workers, unemployment would be climbing. It isn’t.

The unemployment rate was 4.4% in September 2025 and 4.2% in September 2026.4 Over the same year, the civilian labor force shrank by roughly 1 million people, from about 171.3 million to 170.3 million.5 When the pool of workers is shrinking, an economy doesn’t need many new jobs to keep unemployment steady. Oxford Economics has estimated that the “break-even” pace of job growth needed to hold unemployment stable is now close to zero.6

“So a 30,000 jobs print is fine now?” In isolation, it’s far less alarming than it would have been when the labor force was still growing, and new workers needed new jobs. What hasn’t changed is the direction of travel. A shrinking number is still a shrinking number, and as I’ve written before in The Sahm Rule, Employment, And Recession Indicators, it’s the change in unemployment, not the level of hiring, that has historically marked the turn.

The Workers Are Disappearing, Not The Jobs

The biggest reason for the shrinking labor force is demographic, and it’s been building for years.

Participation among Americans 55 and older climbed from 32.3% in 2000 to a peak of 40.7% in 2013. The leading edge of the baby boom was working longer than prior generations.7 That cohort is now leaving. Participation fell to 36.9% in September 2026, down from 38.0% just a year earlier. Slower immigration adds to it. Oxford Economics expected net inflows could fall to as little as 160,000 a year, from more than 3 million a few years ago.6

This is where I part company with the view that jobless growth is primarily an AI story. AI is real, and it plays a role, but the arrow runs the other way. When the labor force stops growing, businesses have only two ways to keep expanding: move the work offshore or replace it with technology. Automation is the response to a shrinking workforce, not the sole cause of it. Both responses are disinflationary over time, which fits the broader case I made in Bad Inflation Cures Itself. Good Inflation Doesn’t.

Where The Bears Have A Point

The other side of this argument has real merit. A “low-hire, low-fire” labor market is stable only as long as the “low-fire” part holds. Companies that aren’t hiring also aren’t building a cushion, and if layoffs start, there’s little momentum in hiring to absorb them.

“The labor market is the main firewall against a recession.” – Michael Pearce, Oxford Economics, quoted in Fortune, February 2026

There’s also a white-collar wrinkle. Gad Levanon of the Burning Glass Institute found that employment in finance, insurance, information, and professional services peaked in November 2022, even as output continued to rise. He called AI-enabled automation a “plausible contributor.”6 Those are well-paid jobs, and their incomes drive a disproportionate share of consumer spending. Throw in four negative payroll months in the past year, and the bears aren’t making things up. They’re reading the same data I am. They just draw a darker conclusion from a pattern that, so far, has kept unemployment near 4%.

Can Productivity Carry The Economy?

The math of growth is simple. Output equals the number of workers times what each one produces. If the first number is flat or falling, everything rides on the second.

As shown, productivity rose 2.2% over the year to the second quarter of 2026, slightly above its 2.0% average since 1965.8 That’s healthy, but it isn’t a boom, and it sets a ceiling. An economy with a flat workforce and 2% productivity growth has a speed limit of roughly 2% real growth, no matter what the AI headlines promise.

That ceiling matters for both sides of the market. For corporations, producing more with the same headcount improves margins. For households, it’s a mixed bag. Total wage income grows more slowly when the number of wage earners isn’t growing. Consumer spending then leans harder on raises for existing workers and on the stock market. Economist Byron Gangnes at the University of Hawaii estimated in October that the AI buildout’s direct contribution to growth has been small. The bigger effect, he found, has come through the stock market’s wealth effect on spending.9 I covered how fragile that channel can be in Wealth Effect Increases And Recession Risks.

“Jobless growth used to mean nobody was hiring. Now it means nobody is left to hire, and that is a very different problem.”

What Jobless Growth Means For Investors

I’m reasonably confident the shrinking labor force is a multi-year trend, not a blip. Boomers aren’t coming back to work. That makes jobless growth more likely to be the norm than the exception for the rest of this decade. What I’m less confident about is how smoothly the economy adjusts. A market that depends on asset prices for consumer spending is only as stable as those prices.

A few practical points follow from that view. First, stop reading weak payroll numbers as a recession signal on their own. With break-even job growth near zero, the unemployment rate and jobless claims are far better gauges. Second, separate the economy from earnings. Productivity-driven growth can support corporate margins even when hiring is flat. Third, keep an eye on the consumer. When incomes grow slowly, spending becomes more sensitive to a drop in the stock market, and that feedback loop runs in BOTH directions.

The trade-off is real. In my view, a disinflationary, slower-growth backdrop tends to favor high-quality bonds over aggressive growth bets, but it also means an economy with less room for error if a shock arrives. Such is the price of growing without new workers: steadier inflation, thinner cushions.

Bottom Line

Today's jobless growth reflects a shrinking workforce more than a collapsing economy, so investors should watch unemployment, productivity, and the wealth effect rather than the payroll headline.

The economy can keep growing without new workers. It just can’t afford to lose the ones it has.

Questions This Article Answers

What is jobless growth?

Jobless growth is a period in which the economy expands, measured by real GDP, while employment barely rises. In the year to mid-2026, real GDP grew by 2.2% while payroll employment grew 0.3%. Historically, it appeared after recessions, in the early 1990s, the early 2000s, and after 2009.

Is jobless growth a sign of a coming recession?

Not on its own. Past episodes saw unemployment between 5.6% and 9.1%, but in 2026 unemployment was 4.2% and falling, as the labor force shrank by roughly 1 million people. A rising unemployment rate is a more reliable warning sign than weak hiring.

Why is the US labor force shrinking?

Baby boomers are retiring, and immigration has slowed. Labor force participation among Americans 55 and older fell from 38.0% in September 2025 to 36.9% in September 2026, down from a peak of 40.7% in 2013.

How can the economy grow without adding jobs?

Through productivity, meaning more output per hour worked. Nonfarm productivity rose 2.2% in the year to mid-2026, slightly above its 2.0% average since 1965. With a flat workforce, that productivity rate sets a rough ceiling on real growth.

Sources & Notes

  1. U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Real Gross Domestic Product (GDPC1), via FRED. Q2 2025 to Q2 2026 change calculated by RIA Advisors. Accessed Oct. 25, 2026.

  2. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, All Employees, Total Nonfarm (PAYEMS), via FRED. June 2025 to June 2026 change and the 12-month average through September 2026 calculated by RIA Advisors. Accessed Oct. 25, 2026.

  3. Yahoo Finance, “Stock market today,” market coverage of October 23, 2026, reporting American Express plans to cut about 5% of its workforce, or 3,500 roles.

  4. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, The Employment Situation, September 2026, released October 2, 2026, and Unemployment Rate (UNRATE) via FRED.

  5. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Civilian Labor Force Level (CLF16OV), via FRED. Household survey levels include annual population control adjustments each January, so year-over-year changes in levels are approximate. The direction matches the participation data.

  6. Jason Ma, “Jobless expansion,” Fortune, February 13, 2026, citing Oxford Economics (Michael Pearce) and the Burning Glass Institute (Gad Levanon).

  7. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Labor Force Participation Rate, 55 Years and Over (LNS11324230), via FRED. Accessed Oct. 25, 2026.

  8. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Nonfarm Business Sector: Labor Productivity (OPHNFB), via FRED. Average annual change since 1965 calculated by RIA Advisors. Accessed Oct. 25, 2026.

  9. Byron Gangnes, “Would we be in a recession without AI?” University of Hawaii Economic Research Organization (UHERO), October 21, 2026.

  10. Replication note: All four charts and the comparison table were built from FRED series GDPC1, PAYEMS, UNRATE, CLF16OV, LNS11324230 and OPHNFB, pulled October 25, 2026. Growth rates compare second-quarter (GDP, productivity) and June (payrolls) values. Monthly payroll changes for July, August and September 2026 match the revised figures in the BLS September Employment Situation. The 2.2% real GDP figure matches the four-quarter growth rate cited by UHERO.
