data.title: Is Trend Still Your Friend?
data.description:
Trend following is one of the oldest and most persistent anomalies in finance. The evidence that recent winners continue to outperform recent losers has been documented across virtually every liquid asset class, stretching back at least two centuries. It stands in direct opposition to the Efficient Market Hypothesis, yet it has survived out-of-sample testing, multiple market regimes, and decades of institutional capital deployed to exploit it.

However, something changed around 2008-09. A July 2026 paper, “Is Trend Still Your Friend? A Microstructural Account of the Demise of Short-Term Trend-Following,” by Jutta Kurth, Zoltan Eisler, Adam Rej, and Jean-Philippe Bouchaud, takes on a puzzling development in systematic investing: why short-term trend-following, reliable for decades, essentially stopped working after the Global Financial Crisis, while longer-horizon trend signals kept delivering. Their answer is not what most practitioners have assumed.

The Puzzle

The authors point to the SG CTA Index — the standard industry benchmark for large commodity trading advisors. After roughly a decade of steady gains, the index has been flat to negative for the better part of fifteen years, rescued only by two macro-driven episodes in 2014 and during the COVID shock.

Rebased) SG CTA Index, 2000–2025. Data courtesy of Société Générale Prime Services & Clearing.

The results are hypothetical results and are NOT an indicator of future results and do NOT represent returns that any investor actually attained. Indexes are unmanaged and do not reflect management or trading fees, and one cannot invest directly in an index.

The following chart shows the 5-20 day exponentially weighted (more weight given to the more recent days and less to the older days, with the weights decaying exponentially) moving average (EWMA).

The results are hypothetical results and are NOT an indicator of future results and do NOT represent returns that any investor actually attained. Indexes are unmanaged and do not reflect management or trading fees, and one cannot invest directly in an index.

Using their own methodological proxy built from about 100 liquid futures contracts across commodities, equity indices, currencies, and government bonds spanning 1995–2025, the authors confirm the same pattern with far more resolution.

Four empirical facts anchor the analysis and constrain any credible explanation:

  1. The break is abrupt — a regime shift, not a gradual decay of alpha.

  2. It is speed-dependent — fast trend signals (days to weeks) were hit hardest, while slow trend signals were largely unaffected.

  3. It is asset-class heterogeneous — equity indices and currencies were hit hard; yields and most commodities were largely spared.

  4. There has been no recovery, despite meaningfully improved liquidity and reduced CTA participation since 2018.

Four Candidate Explanations, Three of Which Fail

The authors test four hypotheses for what broke.

Capacity constraints. The idea that too much capital chasing the same signal eroded returns doesn’t hold up on close inspection. CTA industry assets grew through the 2000s and didn’t peak until 2022 — years after trend profit and loss (P&L) had already gone flat, the wrong sequencing for a crowding story. Liquidity in these markets rose sharply after 2018, which should have relieved any capacity constraint, yet performance never recovered. And when the authors recompute returns using same-day execution — effectively removing a full day of market impact and the associated costs — fast-signal performance is still flat after 2008. If capacity and execution costs were the culprit, stripping those costs out should restore profitability. It doesn’t. That’s an important clue: something happened to the underlying signal, not just the cost of harvesting it.

Electronification of futures markets. The shift from floor trading to electronic order books is a popular culprit, but the timing and sequencing don’t match. Electronification was gradual; the P&L break was sudden. Equity futures electronified more than five years before the break; interest-rate futures electronified early, yet never degraded at all.

A shift in CTA-versus-order-flow dynamics. The authors also examine whether a change in how CTA trades interact with aggregate market order flow explains the pattern. It doesn’t map cleanly onto which asset classes degraded and which didn’t.

The Variable That Actually Matters: Volatility-Normalized Tick Size

Having ruled out the usual suspects, the authors identify the variable that cleanly separates contracts whose trend signals survived from those that didn’t: the tick size of a contract, scaled by its volatility. Sorting the futures universe into “small-tick” and “large-tick” halves each month produces a stark dichotomy. Short-term trend P&L on small-tick contracts collapsed to essentially zero after 2008 across every signal speed tested. On large-tick contracts, performance barely budged — continuing to accrue at close to the pre-2009 rate even at the fastest signal horizons.

Notably, sorting by liquidity instead of tick size — despite the two being correlated — does not reproduce this clean separation. Nor does sorting by asset class on its own; the asset-class pattern turns out to be a byproduct of the fact that equity indices and currencies happen to cluster in the small-tick tier, while bonds and most commodities cluster in the large-tick tier.

Two further cuts of the data corroborate the framework. Trend gains have always been concentrated in low-volatility periods (a long-documented pattern known as the LeBaron effect—a negative (inverse) relationship between volatility and serial correlation of returns: when volatility is high, serial correlation tends to be low, and when volatility is low, serial correlation tends to be higher—and small-tick contracts continue to behave like large-tick contracts specifically during those low-volatility stretches — exactly what you’d expect if the ratio of tick size to volatility, not tick size alone, is what matters. And when the data is split by the magnitude of daily returns, the P&L earned on small, quiet trading days has been essentially untouched by the entire episode. It’s specifically the large, high-conviction directional moves — the ones that used to be trend-following’s bread and butter — where profitability vanished on small-tick contracts.

The Mechanism: A Broken Feedback Loop

Here the paper offers its most interesting contribution. The authors argue that trend following isn’t simply a static anomaly that traders harvest — it’s sustained by a self-reinforcing feedback loop. Trend signals prompt directional trades; those trades push prices further in the signal’s direction through market impact; that price movement sustains or strengthens the signal for the next trader to act on. Profitability and the very existence of the trend anomaly are, in this telling, two sides of the same coin. Break the loop, and both profitability and the signal itself should decay together — not just the harvest, but the underlying pattern.

What broke the loop, in the authors’ account, is the post-crisis takeover of market making by high-frequency trading firms operating on tight, flat-inventory mandates rather than the bank-affiliated and proprietary desks of prior decades that were willing to hold overnight risk. HFT market makers are structurally disinclined to absorb the kind of large, predictable, directional flow that CTA rebalancing generates—the literature on this point (HFTs withdrawing liquidity in front of large institutional orders) is well established.

That withdrawal happened across both tick-size tiers, but its consequences diverged sharply based on order book structure. Small-tick order books are inherently sparse — the economics of queue priority mean depth is naturally thin, so when HFT liquidity providers pulled back, there simply wasn’t enough residual depth left for trend followers to execute without materially “walking the book.” Faced with that cost, trend followers appear to have structurally disengaged from fast signals in those contracts — and once that flow disappeared, so did the impact-driven reinforcement that had been sustaining the trend signal in the first place. Large-tick order books, by contrast, are inherently dense, with meaningful resting depth at multiple price levels; residual liquidity there remained sufficient for trend followers to keep executing much as before, the loop kept turning, and both the signal and its profitability survived.

The authors also examined whether switching from aggressive market orders to passive limit orders offers an escape route on small-tick contracts. It doesn’t. A resting limit order tied to a trend signal gets filled preferentially in the wrong states of the world—filled when the market moves against the position, missed when it runs in the signal’s favor—which simply relabels the cost as missed opportunity rather than slippage. And passive orders, by definition, don’t generate the aggressive flow that feeds the self-reinforcing impact loop in the first place. There’s no execution style that sidesteps the underlying microstructural shift.

A Few Caveats Worth Flagging

Before turning to takeaways, as Max Martone noted in his LinkedIn post on the paper, a few caveats are worth naming. Two of the four authors, Rej and Bouchaud, are affiliated with Capital Fund Management, a large systematic manager whose book leans toward diversified, large-tick trend exposure—a microstructural explanation that vindicates that positioning over a capacity/crowding story is, at minimum, convenient for the firm, even if that doesn’t make the finding wrong. The supporting evidence for the mechanism is also less tidy than the headline P&L break suggests: the paper dates the P&L collapse to roughly 2008-09, but the book-imbalance correlation offered as corroboration doesn’t flip until around 2010, the adverse-selection evidence doesn’t flatten until 2011, and the trade-imbalance correlation shift is dated to 2015—four different break points folded into a single causal story. The small-tick/large-tick dichotomy itself is softer than the headline charts imply: the authors’ own robustness checks show the relationship behaves more like a continuous gradient than a clean binary split, meaning some of the crispness in the main results owes to where the median split happens to fall each month. And the central causal claim—that a shift toward HFT market making specifically drove the change in liquidity provision—isn’t directly evidenced in the data; no HFT participants are identified, and the authors acknowledge they can’t distinguish a change in who is providing liquidity from a change in how existing providers behave. None of this overturns the paper’s core empirical finding, which is well documented: small-tick and large-tick contracts diverged sharply after 2008. It does mean the explanation for why is more provisional than the confident framing suggests.

Key Investor Takeaways

The degradation of short-term trend appears structural, not cyclical. The authors see no obvious mechanism by which it reverses absent a genuine change in market-making structure—new regulation, a new class of inventory-tolerant liquidity providers, or a shift in tick-size regimes. That’s a meaningfully different diagnosis than “the trade got crowded and will eventually work again.”

Not all trend is created equal. Longer-horizon trend signals have held up far better than short-horizon ones, and the driver isn’t asset class so much as the underlying market microstructure—specifically, whether a contract’s order book is naturally sparse or dense relative to its volatility. Investors evaluating CTA managers or trend strategies should pay attention to what signal speeds and instrument mix a given strategy relies on, rather than assuming “trend” is a monolithic exposure.

Capacity discussions should happen at a finer level than the industry aggregate. Because the binding constraint operates tier by tier rather than strategy-wide, a fund’s overall participation rate can look comfortably below historical norms while still being effectively capacity-constrained within the small-tick subset of its book.

This is a good reminder of a broader lesson in evidence-based investing: market structure evolves, and strategies whose returns depend on specific liquidity-provision arrangements can see those arrangements change beneath them. The rise of HFT market making has reshaped a lot more than equity market microstructure—this paper is a well-documented example of how it can quietly erode a return premium that had persisted for roughly two centuries.

As always, the paper leaves open questions the authors themselves flag—most notably how much of trend’s historical existence owes to this impact-driven feedback loop versus more traditional behavioral explanations like slow information diffusion or underreaction to news. That distinction matters for how durable slower-horizon trend premiums are likely to be going forward, and it’s an area worth watching as more research emerges.

data.title: Australia Inflation At 4.9%: What Drove It And Why The Australian Dollar Stayed Flat
data.description:
Australia inflation rose to 4.9% in the 12 months to October 2026, up from 4.3% in September, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported on 25 November. The trimmed mean, the underlying measure the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) uses, rose to 3.8%, and both figures beat forecasts. The Australian dollar closed the day almost where it started. This article breaks down what drove the jump, what it means for the RBA, why the currency barely moved and what the AUD/USD chart shows.

TL;DR

  1. Annual CPI rose to 4.9% in October from 4.3%; the trimmed mean rose to 3.8% from 3.6%. Forecasts were 4.7% to 4.8% and 3.6%.

  2. Housing and transport added 2.58 percentage points, a little over half of the 4.9%. Electricity rose 25.2% and automotive fuel 32.5%.

  3. AUD/USD closed at 0.6634 on 25 November, 0.06% above the day before. Analysts point to copper, the current account and a cooling economy; the next RBA meeting is on 7-8 December.

  4. On the four-hour chart AUD/USD trades in a descending channel. The educational scenario sells at 0.6710 with a stop at 0.6735 and a target of 0.6500.

Australia Inflation in October: The Numbers

The figure is the monthly consumer price index for October, released at 11:30 AEDT on 25 November. It is the annual rate over 12 months, and prices in October alone rose 0.5%, or 0.7% after seasonal adjustment.

Australia CPI for October 2026 against September and against forecasts

Sources: ABS for the results, FXStreet for the forecasts. The two forecasts for the headline differ by 0.1 point, and the result beat both.

What Is Behind the 4.9%

Two groups did most of the work. The ABS table of contributions shows how many percentage points each group added to the annual rate.

Housing and transport added 2.58 of the 4.9 points

Contribution to annual CPI, percentage points, 12 months to October 2026. Groups as published by the ABS.

Contribution of each group to Australia's annual CPI to October 2026, percentage points

  1. Housing prices rose 6.4%; the main contributors were electricity (+25.2%), new dwellings (+5.1%) and rents (+3.5%).

  2. Transport prices rose 10.6%; automotive fuel (+32.5%) was the main contributor.

  3. Food prices rose 3.5%; meals out and takeaway food (+4.1%) was the main contributor.

Values rounded from the ABS table (housing 1.3812, transport 1.1996). The groups shown add up to 4.62 points.

Source: ABS, Consumer Price Index, Australia, October 2026. Data as of 25 November 2026.

The two largest contributors are housing and transport, and the biggest price rises inside them are electricity and fuel. The ABS links the electricity rise to the end of last year's government rebates, which lowered bills a year ago, so part of the annual jump is a comparison with a subsidised base. Fuel follows the oil price. Together, housing and transport account for 2.58 points, about 53% of the annual rate by our arithmetic.

Why the Trimmed Mean Matters More for the RBA

The trimmed mean leaves out the items with the largest price moves each month, and fuel is outside it, which the ABS gives as the reason for the gap between 4.9% and 3.8%. The RBA uses this measure to judge underlying inflation.

In its November Statement on Monetary Policy, published after it raised the cash rate by 0.25 points to 4.85%, the RBA forecast headline inflation of 4.5% and a trimmed mean of 3.6% for December 2026. October already runs above both: by 0.4 point on the headline and 0.2 point on the trimmed mean. The bank expects both measures to stay above 3% until the end of 2027.

October inflation already runs above the RBA's December forecast on both measures

Annual rate, %. Bar: October 2026 actual. Dark tick: RBA forecast for December 2026.

Australia annual CPI and trimmed mean in October 2026 against the RBA forecast for December 2026, %

Source: ABS (October 2026 CPI, 25 November 2026), RBA Statement on Monetary Policy, November 2026. Data as of 25 November 2026.

TD Securities, quoted by FXStreet, calculates the trimmed mean at an annualised 4% over three months and 3.8% over six months. It calls talk of rate cuts in the first half of 2027 premature and expects a long pause, with a further hike unlikely because the economy is cooling.

Why the Australian Dollar Stayed Flat

A higher inflation reading usually supports a currency, because it raises the odds of higher rates. AUD/USD closed 25 November at 0.6634, 0.06% above the close of 24 November, after trading between 0.6560 and 0.6663 during the day.

AUD/USD closed within 0.25% of the previous day on each day from 23 to 26 November

Daily change in the AUD/USD close, %, 23 to 26 November 2026.

Daily change in the AUD/USD close, %, 23 to 26 November 2026

  1. On the CPI day the pair traded between 0.6560 and 0.6663 and closed 0.06% higher.

Change = close / previous close - 1, our arithmetic. The 20 November close of 0.6656 is the base for 23 November. From 20 to 26 November the pair lost 0.42%.

Source: Yahoo Finance, AUD/USD daily history. Data as of 26 November 2026. Past results do not guarantee future performance.

Analysts give different reasons for the flat reaction, and the two can work at the same time.

Why the Australian dollar did not rise after the October CPI: two explanations from banks, 25 November 2026

The US side adds weight. After US core PCE inflation of 3.3%, markets priced about a 97% chance of a 0.25-point Federal Reserve hike in December, FXStreet reported.

What the Market Prices for the RBA

The figures on the RBA's next move come from different sources and dates, and they do not form one picture:

  • Before the November decision, markets priced about 1.5 more hikes by mid-2027 (RBA Statement on Monetary Policy).

  • After the CPI, the chance of a cut in March fell to 13% from 25% (BBH, 25 November).

  • A first cut is not fully priced until August, with about 75% on June (Reuters, as cited by FXStreet).

The second and third items point the same way: a first cut is not expected soon. That matches the TD view of a long pause.

AUD/USD Technical Analysis After the CPI Release

On the four-hour chart AUD/USD trades in a descending channel. An inverted hammer formed at the lows near 0.6560, and the pair rebounded to the upper line of the channel and the upper Bollinger band. There it formed a hanging man, a reversal pattern that can mark the end of the rebound. On 27 November the price stood at 0.6670.

AUD/USD Support and Resistance Levels

AUD/USD H4: descending channel, the inverted hammer at the lows and the hanging man at the upper Bollinger band. Source: RoboForex. Past performance is not indicative of future results.

AUD/USD

support and resistance levels, H4, 27 November 2026

AUD/USD Trade Scenario: Selling at the Channel Line

The scenario places a sell limit order at 0.6710, above the current price. It waits for the rebound to reach the upper line of the channel, and until that happens there is no entry.

AUD/USD trade scenario parameters, educational example

If the hanging man plays out without a pullback, the pair may fall straight to 0.6565, and the sell limit order is not triggered. On the way to 0.6500 the 0.6565 support may slow the decline. The RBA meeting on 7-8 December falls inside the order's validity and can move the pair sharply in either direction. This is an educational example of how entry, stop and target are set around chart levels, and it carries the forecast disclaimer at the end of the article.

Dates to Watch

The RBA meets on 7-8 December, before the November CPI on 6 January

  1. 7-8 December 2026

    RBA Monetary Policy Board meeting

    Cash rate 4.85%

  2. 6 January 2027

    Monthly CPI for November

    Compare with 4.9% and 3.8%

  3. 27 January 2027

    CPI for December

    RBA forecast: 4.5% and 3.6%

  4. 8-9 February 2027

    First RBA meeting of 2027

    With two more CPI releases in hand

Source: RBA board meeting schedule and ABS release calendar, checked 27 November 2026.

The December meeting comes before any new inflation data, so the October figures are the latest the board will see. The January releases then test the RBA's own December forecast of 4.5% and 3.6%. For the mechanics of how inflation data feeds into rate decisions, see our guides on CPI and on how interest rates work. The RoboForex Market Analysis section publishes regular forecasts on major pairs.

Conclusion

Australia inflation stands at 4.9%: housing, where electricity rose 25.2% after the end of rebates, and transport, where fuel rose 32.5%, supplied 2.58 of the 4.9 points. The trimmed mean at 3.8% is the figure that matters for the RBA, and it already runs 0.2 point above the bank's December forecast. Analysts name copper, the current account and a cooling economy as reasons the Australian dollar barely moved, and markets price a Fed hike in December. The RBA meeting on 7-8 December and the November CPI on 6 January are the next tests. On the four-hour chart AUD/USD stays in a descending channel, and the scenario waits for a return to 0.6710 to sell toward 0.6500.

data.title: AUDUSD Attempts Recovery Ahead Of China PMIs
data.description:
Commodity currencies have come under renewed pressure this week, with the Aussie feeling the brunt of new geopolitical tensions. Both the NZD and AUD have had a bit of a breather on Thursday and Friday amid thin trading as institutional traders are mostly away from their desks. However, traders are looking to Monday for the release of key Chinese data that could determine the trajectory of antipodean currencies and others like the yen and CAD.

The proximate cause of the AUDUSD falling to lows not seen since last year was the announcement that the US was looking to raise tariffs on China once again. The new taxes could double the levies to 40% if the trade truce between the two countries were to collapse before its expiry on January 10. The fear of trade escalation caused a shift away from risk, strengthening the greenback at the expense of commodity currencies. However, it was just the latest move in a long-standing trend that has left traders increasingly concerned.

AUD Weighted by Metals Drop

Both the Aussie and Kiwi have been trapped in a push-and-pull between policy and economic indicators. On Friday, Beijing officials promised stronger measures to stabilise financial markets. The collapse of the AI trade has put pressure on the Shanghai stock market and weighed on commodities. The announcement has helped support commodity currencies, as it’s expected to bolster domestic demand.

In the medium term, the AUD has been under increased pressure as iron ore prices fell below $90/ton. Iron ore represents around 20% of Australia’s exports and is a major driver of Aussie dollar buying. Markets are also paying close attention to the sharp drop in copper (down 20% over the last 30 days) as a barometer of industrial growth and AI data center capital expenditure. Analysts suggest that the sell-off has dragged the AUDUSD down by more than 6.4% since September.

What the Market is Looking For

Since the downward trend was driven by concerns over China’s economic outlook, data on economic performance will be key to gauging whether a trend reversal or a plunge lower is imminent. The most important leading indicator, PMI, will be published on Monday, with traders closely watching the difference between the official (NBS) and private (RatingDog) measures.

The NBS tracks a narrower range of larger, state-associated enterprises that are more exposed to the domestic market and are large commodity buyers. These entities are also seen as more responsive to government stimulus programs. RatingDog tracks a broader range of smaller, more export-oriented companies and has recently been buoyed by demand for AI infrastructure.

What China PMIs Are Expected to Show

First out is China’s November NBS Manufacturing PMI, expected to improve to 49.7 from 49.3 previously, but remain below 50, indicating a contraction. Last month’s reading was surprisingly low, and a drop below 49 could signal deteriorating conditions. While that might be negative for the outlook, it would increase pressure on authorities in Beijing to ramp up stimulus. If that happens, the market might counterintuitively rise in a “worse is better” scenario.

On Tuesday, the private RatingDog November Manufacturing PMI comes out, expected to advance into expansion at 52.3, up from 52.0 prior. Markets will be paying close attention to the new export orders sub-index to see whether factories are seeing temporary growth from “front-loaded” orders ahead of potential US tariffs.

Key Summary

  • Bitcoin (BTC.X) staged a modest rebound above $60,000 on November 27, 2026, gaining 0.76% in 24 hours.

  • US spot Bitcoin Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) have recorded a historic $5.39 billion in net outflows for November through November 25.

  • A massive $6.8 billion in Bitcoin options are set to expire today, adding potential volatility to the market.

Why is Bitcoin Surging This Week Despite Such Heavy Selling?

Bitcoin's current resilience above the $60,000 mark comes amidst unprecedented institutional selling pressure from US spot ETFs. This creates a core tension in the market, as the cryptocurrency appears to be finding temporary support from other factors, such as short liquidations, ahead of a major derivatives event.

Record ETF Outflows Weigh Heavily

US spot Bitcoin Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) have experienced a historic month of redemptions, with net outflows reaching an alarming $5.39 billion through November 25, 2026. This figure far surpasses the previous monthly record of $4.51 billion set in June 2026 (according to KuCoin's data).

On November 25 alone, these funds saw approximately $453.1 million in net withdrawals, extending a seven-day streak of continuous outflows. Notably, BlackRock's Bitcoin ETF contributed significantly to this trend, recording $329.7 million in outflows on the same day.

$6.8 Billion Options Expiry Adds Volatility

Today, November 27, 2026, marks a significant event for Bitcoin as approximately $6.8 billion worth of Bitcoin options contracts are slated to expire on Deribit, a major cryptocurrency options exchange.

Such large-scale expiries often introduce heightened volatility into the market as traders adjust their positions and hedge against potential price movements.

The maximum pain level for these expiring options is reportedly around $70,000, though Bitcoin currently trades well below this level.

Short Squeeze Provides Temporary Lift

Despite the overwhelmingly bearish sentiment stemming from ETF outflows, Bitcoin received a short-term boost from significant short liquidations.

Over the past 24 hours, roughly $47 million in Bitcoin short positions were liquidated, considerably outweighing the $18.5 million in long positions closed.

These forced closures, where traders betting on price declines are compelled to buy back Bitcoin to cover their positions, likely contributed to the cryptocurrency's modest rebound.

Analyst Warns of Miner Capitulation

The sustained period of price weakness has placed immense pressure on Bitcoin miners. Analysis from JPMorgan suggests that the average cost to mine one Bitcoin is estimated at approximately $86,000, which is about 30% higher than current market prices.

This significant disparity is leading to signs of "capitulation" among miners, who may be forced to sell their holdings to cover operational costs, potentially adding further selling pressure to the market.

Anton Tsarenok, ViaBTC's Business Development Director, said on November 27, 2026, that:

"Mining competition in 2026 is no longer just about hashrate. It also depends on operational efficiency and capital management."

Technical Indicators

Bitcoin's price action on November 27, 2026, shows it hovering above the psychological $60,000 level, but it remains significantly below its 200-day moving average of $74,516.

The market has recently observed a "death cross" signal in mid-to-late November, where the 50-day moving average crossed below the 200-day moving average, a technical pattern often interpreted as indicating a bearish long-term trend.

The Fear & Greed Index, a popular measure of crypto market sentiment, has slipped into "extreme fear" territory, reflecting the prevailing market anxiety.

Resistance: $62,000, $64,000

Support: $57,500, $53,000

  • Monitor the immediate impact of the $6.8 billion options expiry today. The resolution of these contracts could introduce further volatility or provide clearer directional momentum for the short term.

  • Consider the critical support at $57,500. A definitive break below this level could open the door to a test of $53,000, which represents the average acquisition price for many current Bitcoin holders.

data.title: Jensen Huang’s Comeback Can’t Save A Market Built On Circular AI Financing
data.description:
“Smart people focus on the right things.” – Jensen Huang, Nvidia (NVDA) CEO (retread)

Moonshot Bust

The shoe business can be a tough game. The objective is to make good shoes, earn a profit, and enjoy life. Setting money on fire is not the intent.

One shoe company, which specialized in cozy merino wool sneakers, was valued at a massive $4 billion right after its November 2021 initial public offering (IPO). Investors had high hopes for big profits. But by early 2026, it was burning through cash, closing storefronts, and watching its stock price stumble about in the basement around $2 a share.

These days, when you’re a business owner and no one wants to buy your sneakers, you do the next logical thing. You sell off the remaining parts of the shoe business and start renting out artificial intelligence (AI) chips. That’s the playbook used earlier this year by the company formerly known as Allbirds.

In March 2026, it sold off its entire footwear business, brand name, and remaining inventory to American Exchange Group for $39 million. Then, on April 15, 2026, it dropped a press release that made Wall Street go mad as a hatter.

The company announced it had lined up a $50 million financing deal to buy high-performance graphics processing units and lease AI computing power to businesses. It even asked shareholders to eliminate its environmental conservation charter – a fad from 2021 – because running data centers consumes far too much electricity for an ecofriendly mandate.

The business was initially rebranded as NewBird AI before settling on the name Smartbird (BIRD) in June 2026. It trades on the Nasdaq under the ticker BIRD.

The market reaction on the day of the press release was pure insanity. With roughly a fifth of the company’s shares sold short by traders betting on its demise, the sudden AI pivot triggered a violent short squeeze that was fueled by a stampede of retail traders.

In a single trading session, the stock moonshotted roughly 600 percent, spiking from under $2.50 to an intraday peak above $24.31. Over 280 million shares changed hands in a frenzy of speculative euphoria.

At the market close on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, Smartbird shares were sitting right around $1.07. That’s a wipeout of more than 95 percent from its April peak.

Speculative AI Hype

Smartbird’s pivot, no doubt, was an opportunistic market gimmick. Buying and leasing GPUs is one of the most capital-intensive games on the planet. A single high-end server configured with eight Nvidia chips costs upwards of $300,000. Moreover, global data center spending in 2026 has topped $450 billion.

Dedicated cloud infrastructure giants raise billions just to stay competitive. Showing up to a multi hundred-billion-dollar arms race with a $50 million financing line buys a few hundred chips at best. Without proprietary software, deep customer pipelines, or massive economies of scale, a former footwear maker rebranding as a cloud provider looks curiously like the late ‘90s era trick of slapping dot com onto a failing business just to catch a bid.

The collapse of microcap AI dreamers like Smartbird is an entertaining anecdote. Nonetheless, this exact speculative fever is what has been propping up the biggest stocks on earth. And during the week ending November 20, 2026, the hype was finally called into question.

Wall Street closed the week delivering the type of punishment investors have suffered only five other times since World War II. The S&P 500 fell every single trading day of the week, posting four separate drops of one percent or more. The last times the market pulled off that grim feat were during the depths of the October 2008 financial crisis and the week markets reopened after the September 11, 2001, attacks.

By Friday’s closing bell, the S&P 500 had shed roughly $6 trillion in market value over five days, down an official 10 percent from its October 6 record high. The Nasdaq plunged more than 5 percent on Friday alone, erasing its entire gain for 2026. What’s more, the Nasdaq ended just inches away from a full-blown 20 percent bear market.

Semiconductor stocks suffered the worst of the carnage. The PHLX Semiconductor Index plunged 17 percent on the week and lost a third of its value since the end of September.

What makes this selloff especially noteworthy is that it happened during what was supposed to be a celebration week for AI. Nvidia delivered its first earnings report since the scandalous departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang, posting quarterly revenue of nearly $116 billion and more than doubling its top line from a year earlier.

Meanwhile, Anthropic pulled off the largest IPO in history. In a normal market, those twin milestones would have sent tech stocks to the moon. Instead, both stocks sank, dragging the entire semiconductor complex down with them.

The King Returns

Then came Monday, November 23, 2026, and Wall Street delivered one of the wildest plot twists in corporate history. Before the opening bell, Nvidia’s board pulled off a surprise reversal. It officially reinstating co-founder Jensen Huang as president, chief executive officer, and board director.

As you know, just eleven days earlier, Huang had stepped down after reports broke of his extramarital affairs, including a dalliance with a woman linked to Chinese intelligence. The scandal triggered national security alarms in Washington, sparked an SEC accounting probe, and left Nvidia without its leather jacket wearing leader.

Yet after intense behind-the-scenes lobbying, which included President Donald J. Trump personally phoning into a board meeting to push for Huang’s comeback and declaring he posed zero national security risk, the directors caved. To save face, Nvidia announced it would hire a new Chief Compliance Officer while ongoing government investigations play out. Huang will still have to answer questions before Congress in December.

Word of the king’s return sent Wall Street into a mania. On Monday, trading volume exploded to over 772 million shares as Nvidia stock rocketed 31.48 percent to close at $165.05. That single-day surge, Nvidia’s best since May 2003, instantly conjured roughly $950 billion in market value, shattering the all-time record for the largest one-day dollar gain by any company.

Huang’s resurrection didn’t just rescue Nvidia. It resurrected the entire stock market. Semiconductor rivals like AMD (AMD) and Broadcom (AVGO) caught a massive tailwind. Major U.S. indexes staged a furious relief rally. Both the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq notched their biggest single-day percentage gains since April 2025.

By Tuesday, the adrenaline rush had worn off. Nvidia shares took a post-rally breather, dipping a modest 2.4 percent to close at $161.09. The slide continued on Wednesday, as shares dropped another 3.91 percent to finish the session at $149.30 ahead of the Thanksgiving break.

Regardless, the return of Huang, and the AI hype machine, doesn’t solve the underlying fundamentals of the AI business…

Levered Circular Financing

To understand why blockbuster earnings will not save the market, you must peek under the hood to see how this AI boom has actually been funded. Over the past couple of years, a massive web of leverage and circular financing has inflated demand across the tech sector.

Circular financing is an elaborate game of passing the same dollar around a table. For example, if you sell gumballs and you loan your neighbor $100, and he uses the $100 to buy gumballs from you, has real wealth been created?

Chipmakers and cloud giants have poured tens of billions of dollars in equity investments and credit lines into AI model developers and fledgling cloud startups. Those startups then turn right around and use that exact money to buy chips and rent data center capacity from the very companies that funded them.

Research from the Bank for International Settlements revealed that more than half of all investments flowing into AI companies came from other AI companies. Add in mountains of private credit, margin debt, and heavily leveraged hedge funds chasing momentum, and you get a fragile house of cards.

When asset prices start falling, leverage turns from a tailwind into a wrecking ball. Funds that borrowed heavily to load up on semiconductor stocks suddenly face margin calls, forcing them to dump shares at any price just to raise cash.

Nowhere is this reality check clearer than in Nvidia’s own market capitalization. Just seven weeks ago, on October 6, 2026, Nvidia was riding high at a record valuation of nearly $5.9 trillion. By market close on Wednesday (November 25), and even with this week’s massive rally, Nvidia’s market cap had been cut down to roughly $3.6 trillion. Hence, $2.3 trillion in shareholder wealth has been vaporized in less than two months.

We have little doubt that the AI technological revolution is real. The abilities and applications appear to be growing by leaps and bounds. But that doesn’t mean that at this specific juncture it’s a good investment. In fact, at this very moment there are likely much better investments out there.

This selloff is heavily concentrated in mega cap technology and semiconductor businesses. The equal weight S&P 500, which treats a mid-sized industrial or healthcare company the exact same as Nvidia, has held up remarkably well since the end of September. Real businesses outside the AI echo chamber are still trudging along.

There are also possible bargains – diamonds in the rough – to be found. Shares of Western Union (WU), for example, are trading at a price-to-earnings ratio of 6.05 and are paying a dividend yield of 14.80 percent.

This is not a recommendation. We’re highlighting WU as an example, and to ask the question: Is it a bargain or is it a value trap with underlying fundamental problems?

And what about gold? Last we checked, it was going for $3,564 per ounce. Is this a screaming buy?

In the months ahead, those who can separate the wheat from the chaff, and not get distracted by AI hype, stand to scoop up real cash-flowing businesses – and real money – at fire-sale prices while everyone else is busy getting wrecked by tech.

Do your homework, stay selective, and protect your capital.

Doing the Math on $128 Quintillion

The figure works out to roughly one million times the world economy. The IMF puts that economy at about $128 trillion.

SpaceX was worth about $1.7 trillion at Wednesday’s close. Reaching $128 quintillion would mean a gain of roughly 75 million times, which is a lot of zeros.

The planned satellites are called Starmind. They would act as data centers and use lasers to pass data to one another.

SpaceX must put its first working satellite in orbit by November 2033. It must reach 100,000 satellites by November 2035, with the full fleet due by November 2040.

Earlier this month, Musk said SpaceX ordered solar gear from Germany’s Singulus Technologies. The goal is 100 gigawatts in annual output.

data.title: Silver Buyers In India Are Back. Will They Stay?
data.description:
While China kept more of its silver at home in October, India's imports nearly tripled, a sign that demand held back by import rules since May is coming back.

That matters because India relies on imports for most of the silver it uses, and those imports have been restricted since mid-May. October suggests that much of the buying was delayed rather than lost. China, meanwhile, sent less silver abroad, but for ordinary business reasons rather than policy. Whether the two moves together tighten the market for silver is a separate question. November's trade data, due around December 15, will help answer it.

Silver traded at $42.27 an ounce on the morning of November 26, according to USAGOLD's daily report. A day earlier, it had slipped below $40. The trigger was the Fed's preferred measure of underlying inflation, which rose to 3.3% in October. At Golden Meadow®, we track how interest rates and physical demand pull on the price at the same time. Right now rates appear to be pulling harder, with the Fed's next decision due on December 9.

India Came Back to Buy

India started buying silver from abroad again in October. Its imports that month were worth ₹18,634 crore, a crore being ten million rupees. That is nearly three times September's value, on commerce ministry figures reported by JM Financial. It is still 22.5% below October last year.

The government published no tonnage, so I converted the value at October's average price. In my estimate, India brought in roughly 32 to 36 million ounces (Moz). That is close to the monthly pace of the import permits the government issued in late October. Reuters reported those permits at about 6,500 tonnes over six months. That works out to about 35 Moz a month.

In Issue #26, I discussed how India eased its import rules ahead of the festival season. October's trade figures are the first to include those changes.

Indian investors bought through funds as well. Silver exchange-traded funds, which hold metal for investors who buy their shares, took in ₹3,092 crore in India in October. The figure comes from AMFI, the industry body. That is up 57% from September. At domestic prices, it is worth roughly 4.3 to 5.0 Moz, though the funds' own metal purchases might differ. 

China Kept More Silver at Home

China moved the other way. It exported 285.43 tonnes of refined silver in October, about 9.2 Moz, according to Shanghai Metals Market, a Chinese price and data service. Exports for January to October were 15.5% below last year.

Comparing two of its year-to-date totals gives a sharper view of the last three months. On my arithmetic, China's exports from August to October were about 37% lower than a year earlier. That is roughly 18.9 Moz less silver leaving the country.

The reasons are commercial. Buyers inside China wanted the metal, so smelters, the plants that refine it, sold at home for a small premium. Exporting through Hong Kong paid slightly less than the London price, so there was no gain in shipping it out. India's own restrictions had also cut demand from a major customer. I found no evidence that Beijing tightened its export rules.

Sources: JM Financial, India October imports | KNN India, import permits | Kotak Neo, AMFI October flows | Shanghai Metals Market, China silver exports, November 24 | Shanghai Metals Market, China silver exports, July | China Briefing, APEC 2026 | Silver Institute, interim review, November 12

The dollar value converts rupees at about ₹95.5, October's approximate average; the ounce range assumes an October average silver price of $54 to $60. The fund estimate uses domestic prices of ₹2.0 to 2.3 lakh per kilogram, a lakh being 100,000 rupees. The August-to-October China figure subtracts a January-to-July total from an earlier Shanghai Metals Market summary; no October year-on-year figure was published. 

Why the Two Moves Don't Simply Add Up

It is tempting to add India's buying to China's lower exports and call it a squeeze, a sudden shortage of metal available to buy. The numbers don't support that yet.

Some of the silver India bought might have come from China, so the two moves overlap. China's imports also fell by more than half in October. On my arithmetic, its net exports, exports minus imports, rose from September. A full comparison with last year needs import data I don't have.

The full-year forecast also tempers the picture. The interim review from Metals Focus and the Silver Institute still expects Indian bar and coin demand to fall 10% this year. One strong month does not reverse that.

The politics did not change either. Trump and Xi met in Shenzhen on November 19. They announced no tariff changes and no extension of the trade truce, which runs to January 10. Silver was not mentioned in the outcome. 

What This Means to Silver Investors

India's buyers did not walk away from silver. Once the paperwork eased, imports rose to roughly the monthly pace of the new permits. That supports the longer-term case for silver, because India relies on imports for most of the silver it uses.

China's lower exports help less than they first appear. They reflect strong demand at home, which is good for silver, but not a policy decision to hold metal back.

So the verdict is close to neutral for silver right now, with a modest positive from India. The interim review still expects a shortfall of 35 Moz this year. Silver exchange-traded funds worldwide are forecast to release 45 Moz, more than covering it. The price is also responding to interest rates more than to trade flows, as how silver has traded this autumn shows. November's Indian trade data will show whether October was a catch-up month or the start of a steadier pace.

data.title: The ECB’s New Boss Has Timing On His Side
data.description:
Like most things in life, being a successful central banker is as much about timing and luck as experience and skill.

New ECB president Pablo Hernández de Cos has plenty of the latter. And whisper it, but his timing looks rather good, too.

Sure, on the face of it, the inheritance looks grim: inflation at 4%, high energy prices, wobbly stock markets and bond market tensions that haven’t exactly gone away. A December ECB rate hike looks inevitable. But how much of that will still matter when De Cos takes office in February?

By then, inflation may well be past the peak. Maybe it already is. November's unexpectedly soft French and Spanish figures point to a drop in next week's eurozone headline rate. Cheaper petrol is clearly part of this, but French services and Spanish core inflation point to reduced pressure elsewhere, too.

Admittedly, that doesn’t mean inflation is set to drop back immediately. Higher natural gas prices are only now reaching utility bills, which is likely to keep energy's overall contribution to inflation elevated into spring or early summer – even as the impact of high petrol and diesel prices should fade rapidly from March.

Utility bill inflation is only just picking up

In the end, though, this is a bit of a moot point. Four per cent inflation may be an uncomfortable place for central bankers, particularly those who worry about its impact on consumer and business expectations.

But unless you think energy prices will start climbing again in the winter and next spring, then it’s only a matter of time before their impact on inflation starts to wane. Our forecasts have headline inflation undershooting the ECB's target in the second half of 2027.

What really seems to matter now for officials is not so much the level of energy prices at any given time, but what they tell us about the uncertainty surrounding the Iran war. Andrew Bailey at the Bank of England has made it clear this latter point will have a strong bearing on its December decision.

The ECB and BoE rate hikes so far have been partly justified as an insurance against the tail risk that things get very ugly in the energy markets.

Those tail risks do tentatively seem to be fading, though. Sure, a lasting US-Iran agreement feels like a long shot right now. Yet Middle Eastern oil has continued flowing despite attacks on shipping and threats to infrastructure. The longer that continues, the less plausible the worst-case scenarios become, even without a peace deal. I’d argue central bankers should already be starting to think this way at their December meetings.

That thinking is already playing out in energy markets, too. Notwithstanding market moves over the past few days, November has seen a sharp drop in the risk premium baked into crude oil prices. Barring renewed escalation, our energy team expects European gas prices to almost halve by the second quarter, with Brent crude below $80/bbl.

Then there are second-round effects, which are still conspicuous by their absence. Barring the slight increase in core inflation so far, there’s still no strong sign that higher energy prices are bleeding out across the inflation basket. My measure of inflation in energy-intensive categories has still not risen this year:

There's little sign of indirect energy effects on inflation

The ECB seems to agree with this assessment, but officials understandably want more evidence. Firms may have been better placed to absorb the initial shock than in 2022, while gas prices have only recently risen more sharply. The hawks would argue that this resilience can only last so long without companies putting up prices.

But fast-forward another three months, when De Cos takes office, and those arguments will start to look a little thin if there’s still no sign of inflationary pressure outside of energy.

There are two things in particular I’d keep an eye on before then. One is food, where inflation has started to inch higher off a very low base. But neither producer nor import prices point to an imminent spike. Yes, some agricultural commodities are 10-15% above February levels, not helped by this summer's drought. But that's offset by fertiliser prices, which have reversed their initial war-driven surge.

And while we’re on the topic of commodities, industrial metal prices are down on pre-war levels, while shipping costs seem to have peaked too. That should keep a lid on core goods prices.

How commodity prices have fared since February

Agricultural prices based on UNCTAD data. Metals based on S&P GSCI. Shipping based on Baltic/Dewry indicies.

Source: Macrobond, ING

Then there are wages, which also offer little evidence of a broader inflation problem so far. Inflation categories (mostly services) that are sensitive to wage growth have not accelerated this year. The ECB's negotiated-wage tracker does not suggest a material pickup in 2027, either, although plenty of these deals are still yet to be agreed.

Needless to say, none of this guarantees an easy presidency. De Cos will have to decide early on whether another rate hike is needed in March (we currently think it won’t), while navigating an increasingly fraught European political backdrop. Still, he may find that the hardest part of the current inflation fight is already behind him. And for a new central banker, a little bit of good timing never hurts.

James Smith

THINK Ahead in developed markets

United States (James Knightley)

  • Recent equity market volatility and steep gasoline price falls have led financial markets to solidly back the view that the Fed will hike 25bp on 9 December rather than go with 50bp as mooted by Governor Chris Waller. We will get lots of data next week, including the ISM reports, but it will likely need a huge payrolls number with another drop in unemployment to move market pricing meaningfully.

  • ISM Surveys/Jobs Report (Tue/Thu/Fri): Based on regional indicators, we look for both the manufacturing and services ISMs to dip marginally but remain consistent with GDP growth of around 2-2.5%. In terms of payrolls, labour indicators remain consistent with a low-hire, low-fire economy, so we expect a reversal after the robust October print of 165k, predicting 80k with the unemployment rate remaining at 4.1%.

Eurozone (Bert Colijn)

  • November Inflation (Tue): Focus will be on the eurozone November inflation rate next week. Headline inflation has soared in recent months on the back of higher energy inflation, and at 4% in October, the ECB is on high alert. Especially now that the core inflation reading for October was revised up from 2.5% to 2.6% in the second estimate. That means that core inflation has increased by 0.1ppt each month over the past two months, which finally shows some modest early evidence of second-round effects. Still, France and Spain already showed a large decline in November on the back of lower energy prices. And other price categories didn’t see massive moves either. This indicates that overall inflation pressures are still mainly driven by energy, but also that November is likely to see a drop back from 4%.

data.title: Is Oracle The Next Bear Stearns?
data.description:
The Bear Stearns Comparison

On Thanksgiving night, Michael Burry shared a piece with a striking comparison. In its November 20 analysis, Groundbreaker reported that five-year default protection on Oracle cost more than comparable protection on Bear Stearns at the start of 2008.

Groundbreaker’s argument starts with the rent. A developer borrows against what a tenant has promised to pay for a data center. If lenders grow less confident in that tenant, they’ll lend less against the same lease. Take a campus valued at $100 million with $85 million of debt. A 15% drop in its value wipes out the owner’s equity on paper. That can make the next campus harder to finance even if the tenant is still paying on time.

Three Days Versus Three Years

Bear Stearns borrowed against mortgage bonds, much of it overnight. As major lenders stopped renewing those loans, its pool of available cash and liquid assets went from about $18 billion on Monday to $2 billion on Thursday, as shown in a study of the run. That Thursday, it told the Fed it expected to come up short the next day.

Oracle, meanwhile, sold $10 billion in bonds and $10 billion in common stock on November 4. It agreed to pay 7% to 8.65% interest on the bonds, and the earliest of those bonds comes due in 2029, according to its SEC filing. On November 20, the same day Groundbreaker published, Oracle said it had secured the money it needed to fulfill its contract with OpenAI.

Oracle paid up for time and brought in new shareholders to bear part of the risk. It still needs OpenAI to pay for the computing capacity it signed up for. If those payments fall short, Oracle will owe the same interest on its new bonds with less cash coming in.

Who Has To Sell?

The places to look for a 2008-style run are the lenders and funds holding the debt. A lender with long-term funding may be able to hold a troubled loan while the borrower restructures. A fund facing margin calls or withdrawals may have to sell whatever it can, including investments unrelated to AI. Fed Governor Michael Barr singled out leveraged funds as a potential source of forced selling in an AI downturn.

Some losses could also land with the tech companies that helped finance their customers. At a TeraWulf campus in Kentucky, Google agreed to step in if Anthropic defaults on certain data-center leases. Google can pay the overdue rent and take over the lease or, in some circumstances, pay an exit fee. That protection kicks in when the last data hall on the relevant lease starts its term, according to TeraWulf’s filing.

For stock investors, we’d watch two things. First, are companies postponing campuses and chip orders as financing gets more expensive? That matters to Nvidia and its suppliers. Second, are lenders pulling funding from firms that hold AI debt? That’s how trouble at a data center can reach stocks that have nothing to do with AI.

Where We’re Looking Next

CoreWeave looks vulnerable if financing gets tighter. It spent $9.4 billion on capital investment in the third quarter and generated about $2 billion in operating cash flow, according to its latest earnings release.

We’re still bullish on AI names with stronger balance sheets. We’ve lined up a potential trade for today in one company we think could soon get an investment from the U.S. government.

The RSI measures the strength of recent price movements. Readings below 30 generally indicate oversold conditions, while readings above 70 suggest overbought conditions.

CoinShares said the latest reading was close to levels recorded around Bitcoin’s 2022 market trough and among the most oversold in the cryptocurrency’s history.

“It is not a particularly useful indicator in the middle of a trend, but historically it has been much better at identifying exhaustion at extreme price highs or lows,” the report stated.

Bitcoin’s Market Value to Realized Value (MVRV) ratio is also approaching valuation levels associated with major market bottoms in 2015, 2019 and 2022.

MVRV compares Bitcoin’s market capitalization with its realized capitalization, which estimates the value of coins based on the price at which they last moved. Lower readings can indicate that the market is trading closer to the aggregate cost basis of its holders.

“We are not quite at those extremes, but for an investor looking one or two years ahead the valuation is becoming increasingly attractive,” CoinShares added.

The firm cautioned that these indicators do not confirm that Bitcoin has reached its bottom. Instead, they suggest that valuations are becoming more attractive for investors with a longer investment horizon.

AI leverage could expose Bitcoin to wider market stress

CoinShares also highlighted risks surrounding the artificial intelligence (AI) investment trade, particularly leveraged positions and increasingly complex financing structures supporting expectations of high future returns.

If returns from AI investments disappoint, the resulting valuation correction could develop into a liquidity event, forcing investors to sell assets to meet debt obligations.

The report argues that although Bitcoin is not fundamentally tied to the AI sector, both markets draw from the same pool of risk-sensitive capital. This creates the potential for financial stress in one market to spill over into the other.

“If expected returns begin to disappoint, leverage could turn a valuation correction into a liquidity event (a forced sale of assets to meet debts) surprisingly quickly,” the firm said.

Macroeconomic conditions present another obstacle to Bitcoin’s recovery. Stronger-than-expected US personal income and slightly hotter core Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation could keep the Federal Reserve (Fed) cautious about easing monetary policy.

CoinShares cited October personal income growth of 0.7%, above the 0.4% consensus estimate, while core PCE inflation increased 3.3% year over year, exceeding the 3.2% forecast.

The firm also noted that the US Dollar Index (DXY) was approaching a 19-month high, while Treasury yields had retreated from recent highs after briefly moving above 5%. Together, these moves point to tighter financial conditions and growing risk aversion.

However, falling Oil prices could eventually ease inflationary pressure. Oil declined from approximately $113 per barrel in late October to around $97, although CoinShares said the impact could take time to feed through into inflation data.

Despite the challenging environment, CoinShares said Bitcoin’s relative resilience during the latest market stress suggests that “a fair amount of forced selling has already taken place.”

The firm expects Bitcoin to trade broadly between $60,000 and $90,000 until liquidity conditions or monetary policy change more meaningfully.

CoinShares’ outlook points to a potentially slow bottoming process rather than an immediate V-shaped recovery. While oversold momentum and improving long-term valuations could attract investors, persistent macroeconomic pressure and uncertainty surrounding the AI trade may prolong consolidation.

Bitcoin is trading at $59,740, down 1% over the past 24 hours at the time of writing.

data.title: Gold And Palladium: The Comeback Meets Its First Test
data.description:
Remember how things looked on Wednesday? The bears had plenty of reasons to celebrate.

Gold had broken below a major psychological barrier. Silver had challenged an important weekly Fibonacci retracement. Platinum, palladium, and copper were reaching increasingly deep support levels.

It wasn't exactly a comfortable picture for the bulls. But apparently, someone forgot to tell the buyers that the week was already over.

And what a comeback they're attempting!

Fresh bullish gaps have appeared across the metals during the past two sessions, and buyers are now challenging several levels that had previously belonged firmly to the bears.

Yet there's a catch. Reclaiming lost support is one thing. Breaking through the resistance left behind by the previous selloff is another.

Today, gold and palladium provide two particularly interesting examples of that challenge. One is attempting to recover after losing a major psychological barrier. The other is fighting back after briefly falling beneath an important historical low.

Let's see what their charts are telling us.

Gold (GC.F) - A Bullish Comeback Meets Its First Major Test

Gold's buyers have certainly made their presence felt. Remember Wednesday?

The yellow metal had plunged below 3500, challenging an important historical support combination and raising the possibility of another decline toward the 3300 area, but the bears couldn't maintain their advantage.

Gold recovered above 3500, invalidating the immediate intraday breakdown beneath that psychological barrier. Then Thursday's Asian session brought a fresh bullish gap at 3535.80-3583.60. Even though sellers subsequently attempted to push prices lower, the gap wasn't completely filled.

And today's reaction has been considerably stronger.

Gold increased to 3683.65, challenging the bearish gap from November 20 at 3633-3685, which means buyers came within just 1.35 of its upper boundary!

What Could Strengthen the Bullish Case?

The first requirement is a convincing daily close above the recovered support levels.

A Friday close above 3535 would reinforce the invalidation of Wednesday's breakdown beneath 3500 and improve the short-term technical picture. It would also support the developing recovery from the historical green support area marked on the weekly chart.

However, reclaiming the lower boundary of the red declining channel on D1 is a separate technical test. That boundary, together with the November 20 bearish gap, continues to present an important obstacle. If buyers manage to overcome this resistance combination, the recovery would gain a much stronger technical foundation.

Conversely, another rejection beneath these barriers could leave gold vulnerable to renewed selling pressure and with the weekly RSI still relatively weak and Stochastic deeply oversold, the broader structure deserves particular attention.

Daily Takeaway: supports: the bullish gap at 3535.80-3583.60, followed by the psychological 3500 barrier. Key resistance: the November 20 bearish gap at 3633-3685 and the nearby declining-channel boundary. Closing above these barriers would strengthen the recovery scenario.

Bottom Line: Gold has challenged Wednesday's bearish breakdown, but the next important achievement would be converting this impressive rebound into a confirmed recovery above overhead resistance.

Palladium (PA.F) - A Powerful Gap and a Historical Level Reclaimed

Palladium's bulls have delivered one of the week's most dramatic responses.

After Wednesday's decline carried prices through another Fibonacci objective and below the August 2024 low at 813.50, the bearish outlook appeared increasingly demanding for buyers. However, Thursday brought a remarkable change.

A substantial bullish opening gap appeared at 772-859, providing the foundation for a powerful recovery attempt and on Friday, buyers extended their offensive.

Palladium reached 907.75, entering the bearish gap from November 20 at 906-918. Although the recovery subsequently retreated toward 877, the latest price remains above an especially important historical reference. The August 2024 low at 813.50 has been reclaimed, which is potentially significant.

What Would Confirm the Improvement?

If palladium finishes Friday's session above 813.50, it would strengthen the case that the earlier breakdown beneath that historical low has been invalidated. A weekly close above the same level would provide additional confirmation. That would leave buyers with a stronger foundation for another attempt to overcome the 906-918 resistance zone. Beyond that, attention would turn toward the previously broken lower boundary of the red declining wedge visible on W1.

Successfully reclaiming that weekly boundary would be another important step in repairing the technical structure and could eventually open the door to a challenge of the psychological 1000 barrier.

For now, the weekly trend remains weak and the market is still emerging from deeply oversold conditions, but the recovery above 813.50 gives buyers a meaningful level to defend.

Daily Takeaway: key support: 813.50, together with the bullish-gap area at 772-859. Resistances: 906-918, followed by the broken weekly wedge boundary and potentially 1000. Friday's close above 813.50 would strengthen the bullish recovery scenario.

Bottom Line: Palladium has staged a powerful counterattack but transforming that rebound into a sustained technical improvement will require buyers to reclaim more than one previously broken resistance level.

What About the Other Four Markets?

U.S. Dollar - The Bulls Defend Support, but Resistance Still Awaits

While the metals are recovering, the dollar remains inside its orange consolidation. Buyers have successfully defended an important bullish-gap support area, but another bearish gap and a broader weekly resistance combination continue to stand in their way.

Silver - The Bulls Return to the Battlefield

After a dramatic decline earlier this week, silver has reclaimed important support and challenged a bearish gap from November 20. The next question is whether buyers can maintain that improvement and push through the resistance separating them from another psychological barrier.

Platinum - Can the Bulls Reclaim the Weekly Channel?

Platinum has also benefited from renewed buying interest. Its recovery has carried prices back above an important weekly channel boundary and toward nearby daily resistance. Friday's closing result could help determine whether the latest rebound has a stronger technical foundation.

Copper - Buyers Defend an Important Historical Low

Copper has staged its own counterattack, reclaiming several Fibonacci extensions intraday after an unsuccessful attempt to break an important historical low. However, another resistance area remains overhead, making the next closing signals particularly interesting.

Today's Anna's Trading Lab Premium follows the latest developments across all six markets, including the support levels buyers are attempting to reclaim, the resistance areas standing in their way, and the technical conditions that could shape next week's trading. The complete edition also includes our Friday's Cheat Sheet, bringing together the key levels and scenarios worth watching as the market approaches December.

Final Thought - The First Test of a Comeback

There's a detail worth noticing in both gold and palladium today.

Buyers have managed to stage substantial recoveries, reaching resistance areas created during the previous selloff, but on our latest charts, both metals have already retreated from their intraday highs.

That gives us a particularly useful way to evaluate the strength of this comeback. It's not just about how far prices managed to rise. It's also about how much of that recovery buyers can preserve when sellers return near familiar resistance.

Friday's closing candles may help answer that question, while the next attempt to challenge those overhead barriers could reveal whether the bulls are building lasting momentum or still struggling to regain lost territory.

After all, the strength of a comeback isn't always measured by its most impressive moment. Sometimes, it's revealed by what buyers manage to hold onto afterward.

data.title: Ignore Friday's Short Session. Monday Is When The Year Gets Priced.
data.description:
Wall Street loves a holiday bounce because the charts look clean and the headlines write themselves. On Black Friday the whole show wraps by 1 p.m. Eastern, and the trading floor feels more like a skeleton crew than a real market.

My take is simple. This short session does not decide how the rest of the year goes. The people who move real size are already looking past it. Monday is when full desks come back, the order books regain depth, and the next stretch of economic data starts answering questions this market still has not settled.

A half day is not a verdict

U.S. stocks were closed Thursday for Thanksgiving, and Friday is the classic early close. You get about three and a half hours instead of the usual six and a half. Volume on this day often runs near half of a normal session, and sometimes lower than that.

That thin book is the whole point. When fewer institutional players are present, a modest order can push a stock farther than it would on an ordinary Tuesday in March. Spreads widen and false breakouts show up. A green close can feel like renewed confidence when it is really just a quiet room with fewer people arguing over price.

History leans a little green on Black Friday over the long haul, and that is fine as trivia. It is a weak foundation for a year-end investment thesis. In a high-fear stretch, a short day can still swing hard if a headline lands, which the Omicron scare a few years back already proved. The calendar does not make the market honest. Participation does. So if futures are ripping higher into the open, enjoy the color. Do not build your story for the rest of 2026 on three and a half hours of holiday traffic.

What this week already told us

This market staggered into the turkey after a brutal stretch. The S&P 500 had already slipped more than 10% off the early October high and into correction territory. Artificial intelligence names did a lot of the damage. Nvidia's (NVDA) leadership fight, Anthropic's rough first days as a public company, and a broader argument over how much of the AI capital spending is real end demand versus expensive hope all hit at once. Then the holiday week tried to put air back in the tires. By the time Friday futures lit up, the major indexes were looking at a multi-day rebound on the order of about 4% for the week.

That rebound matters as a mood check. It does not close the case. Can the AI complex hold when the full crowd is trading again, and can earnings keep up with the capital thrown at chips and data centers? Holiday liquidity is a terrible place to answer either question.

Monday is the first honest session

Full hours return Monday, November 30. That is when the real auction starts again. I do not mean Monday is magic. I mean it is the first day the people who move size are back in their seats with a full week on the board. Seasonal studies often show the Monday after Thanksgiving giving back some of Friday's cheer once volume returns.

This year the calendar after the holiday is heavier than the leftovers. Next week brings manufacturing and services surveys, private payrolls color, and the November jobs report on December 4. Economists polled around the wires have been looking for something like 90,000 jobs and an unemployment rate near 4.1%. Those figures feed straight into the Federal Reserve meeting on December 8 and 9. Futures markets have been pricing a quarter-point rate increase as a near lock, roughly in the high-90% range on the CME FedWatch tool. The fight is less about whether policymakers move and more about how hard they talk about 2027.

That stack is the real year-end machine: labor strength or softness, wage pressure, and how the committee sounds about inflation that has refused to settle. Layer AI drama back on top. Early December hearings around Nvidia's returned chief executive can reopen the confidence debate overnight. Thin Friday prices will not survive that kind of week if the story turns again.

How I am watching it

As for me, I am treating Friday like weather, not climate. I want Monday and Tuesday to hold the rebound with real volume, not just another gap that fades by lunch. I want market breadth, not only a handful of megacap stocks dragging the averages. I want the jobs report to either confirm a still-firm economy the Fed can lean against or show enough cooling that investors can debate the path without another panic. Holiday futures strength is cheap courage. Holding gains into a Federal Reserve week is different.

None of that is a recommendation to chase Friday's open or to fade a green candle because the calendar says so. It is a reminder that markets tell the truth when capital is present and the next hard data is on the table.

Bottom Line

Black Friday's short session is a thin holiday read with an early closing bell. The rest of 2026 gets priced when full desks return Monday and the market has to live with jobs week and a December Fed that is almost certainly raising rates again.
